Braided Scalar Quantum Electrodynamics


Abstract
We formulate scalar electrodynamics in the braided L ∞ L_{\infty} -algebra formalism and study its perturbative expansion in the algebraic framework of Batalin-Vilkovisky quantization. We confirm that UV/IR mixing is absent at one-loop order in this noncommutative field theory, and that the non-anomalous Ward-Takahashi identities for the braided gauge symmetry are satisfied.

1
Introduction and Summary

Braided field theories were introduced in
[
1
,
2
]
as a novel alternative framework for organising the symmetries and dynamics of noncommutative field theories, motivated by considerations from noncommutative gravity
[
3
,
4
]
. Their quantization was developed in
[
5
,
6
,
7
]
where it was shown that the non-locality due to noncommutativity is manifested in correlation functions in a very different manner than in the standard noncommutative field theories (reviewed in e.g.
[
8
,
9
,
10
]
). Similarly to the earlier systematic approaches of Oeckl
[
11
,
12
,
13
]
, as well as of Grosse and Lechner
[
14
,
15
]
, braided quantum field theory already exhibits non-local effects at the level of free fields through a noncommutative deformation of Wick’s Theorem. A main new impetus is the ability to incorporate theories with gauge symmetries, contrary to the original works which were limited to scalar field theories.

At the level of interacting quantum fields, in all calculations performed thus far, up to two-loop order and three-point multiplicity, the braided theories have been found to be free of the notorious problem of UV/IR mixing
[
16
]
which obstructs renormalisability of the standard models (this feature was anticipated earlier by
[
17
,
18
,
19
]
, however through somewhat adhoc heuristic reasonings). This has sparked the exciting prospect that these non-local models may be well-defined quantum field theories, without the need of modifying their ultraviolet and infrared behaviours
[
20
]
as in the perturbatively renormalisable Grosse-Wulkenhaar model
[
21
,
22
,
23
]
.

By their very definition, braided quantum field theories can only be handled using the framework of homotopy algebras: there is no ‘braided space’ of fields, hence no notions of functional differentiation or path integration and the standard quantization methods do not apply. Even in the commutative case, this algebraic perspective expresses Feynman diagram techniques in a manner that is mathematically precise and conceptually clear, in contrast to the usual textbook approaches (e.g. path integral techniques) whose mathematical foundations are not well-defined. This is not to say that it completely avoids the analytic complications of infinite-dimensional spaces of fields and the standard loop divergences of quantum field theory, but it computes correlation functions and scattering amplitudes in a purely algebraic setting. In the braided noncommutative case, the power of the formalism is even more striking: as a comparison of the results of the naive approach of
[
24
]
with the systematic approach of
[
6
]
shows, braided quantum field theory does not follow the traditional Feynman rules of perturbation theory.

At the classical level, braided field theories are defined by deforming the
L_{\infty}
-algebra which organises the symmetries and dynamics of a given field theory to a novel homotopy algebraic structure called a ‘braided
L_{\infty}
-algebra’ in
[
1
,
2
]
. As
L_{\infty}
-algebras are the natural algebraic structure underlying the Batalin-Vilkovisky (BV) formalism (see e.g.
[
25
,
26
]
for reviews), the quantization of braided field theories is captured by a braided version of BV theory and the homological perturbation lemma, originally developed in
[
5
]
. The purpose of this paper is to explore a new example of braided quantum field theory with gauge symmetry that originates in an
L_{\infty}
-algebra which is more general than a differential graded Lie algebra. At the classical level, the examples of
[
1
,
2
]
demonstrate that these noncommutative field theories differ most profoundly from the standard versions. Our aim here is to explore the extent to which differences occur at the quantum level.

In the following we treat in detail the model of braided scalar quantum electrodynamics (QED), which is the simplest theory of this type, possessing braided
\mathsf{U}(1)
gauge symmetry. From a physical perspective, scalar QED models the type of interactions between weak hypercharge gauge bosons and Higgs bosons in the Standard Model of particle physics; it also provides a simple venue for spontaneous symmetry breaking and the Higgs mechanism in other contexts. From a technical standpoint, its
L_{\infty}
-structure is more complicated than the spinor version of QED considered in
[
6
]
which originates in a differential graded Lie algebra, as it contains a non-zero ternary bracket organising the quartic interaction between scalars and photons. While we shall indeed find a rich classical theory whose gauge symmetry and dynamics drastically differ from both ordinary scalar QED as well as its usual noncommutative deformation with star-gauge symmetry, braided BV quantization produces the same qualitative results as the calculations of
[
6
,
7
]
: we confirm that UV/IR mixing is absent in correlation functions up to one-loop order and three-point multiplicity.

As a novel additional chapter in the story of braided quantum field theory, in this paper we shall also derive algebraic Ward-Takahashi identities satisfied by the correlation functions of braided scalar QED, which are a consequence of the braided gauge invariance of the theory. Our approach is based on the underlying local Becchi-Rouet-Stora-Tyutin (BRST) cohomology within the braided BV formalism and the homological perturbation lemma. These identities are intimate relatives of the algebraic braided Schwinger-Dyson equations derived in
[
7
]
. Our derivation is new, and since it does not rely on the traditional path integral techniques, it is also of broader interest as further development within the homotopy algebraic formulation of general quantum field theories.

Analogously to the standard situation in textbook quantum field theory (see e.g.
[
27
]
), gauge invariance in braided scalar QED is manifested in three ways:

•

At the classical level as a fundamental symmetry which is captured by the Maurer-Cartan theory for the underlying braided
L_{\infty}
-algebra.

•

In the weak conservation law for the electric current that follows from the Noether identity for the braided
\mathsf{U}(1)
gauge symmetry and the Maurer-Cartan equations.

•

At the quantum level in the algebraic Ward-Takahashi identities which follow from homological perturbation theory and impose braided
\mathsf{U}(1)
gauge transformations on correlation functions.

In this paper we develop all three complementary perspectives in detail, thus demystifying some of the unusual features that braided gauge symmetries are known to present
[
1
,
2
]
compared to ordinary gauge symmetries in field theory and star-gauge symmetries in noncommutative field theory.

Outline.

The organisation and main results of the remainder of this paper are as follows.

In
section

2
we formulate classical scalar electrodynamics in the
L_{\infty}
-algebra formalism. By deforming the underlying homotopy algebra to a braided
L_{\infty}
-algebra, we define our classical model of braided scalar electrodynamics using Maurer-Cartan theory. We also derive the classical BV extension of the braided Maurer-Cartan functional.

In
section

3
develop the quantization of braided scalar electrodynamics using extended braided BV theory and the homological perturbation lemma. We derive the interaction vertices and introduce a diagrammatic notation for them as well as for the propagators of the theory. We then explain in detail how to compute correlation functions of polynomial observables in braided homological perturbation theory.

In
section

4
we present explicit calculations of correlation functions using braided homological perturbation theory up to one-loop order. We demonstrate that all one-point functions vanish, as well as that the photon and scalar propagators receive contributions from only planar diagrams. We also compute the scalar-scalar-photon vertex function, showing that it differs from its commutative counterpart only in a noncommutative phase factor depending on the external momenta. Altogether these results show that the correlators of braided scalar QED are free from UV/IR mixing at one-loop.

Finally, in
section

5
we derive our new algebraic Ward-Takahashi identities, which impose braided gauge transformations on correlation functions, and compare our approach with other treatments in the literature based on homotopy algebras. We start by exhibiting the braided BRST symmetry of our theory, and use it to derive the conservation law for correlators of the extended Noether current for the braided
\mathsf{U}(1)
symmetry in the BV formalism. We then use the braided homological perturbation lemma to derive anomalous Ward-Takahashi identities, giving an intrinsic interpretation of the anomaly in terms of the action of the BV Laplacian on the scalar field BRST functional, which vanishes in braided scalar QED. As explicit examples we derive the all loop order relation between the improper three-vertex function and the scalar propagator, as well as transversality of the exact photon vacuum polarisation tensor, checking them explicitly using our one-loop results. We also derive an explicit identity for general correlation functions involving arbitary numbers of external scalars and photons.

Notation and Conventions.

In this paper we work on four-dimensional Minkowski space
\mathbbm{R}^{1,3}
, on which ordinary scalar QED is perturbatively renormalisable.
We use standard coordinates
x=(x^{\mu})=(x^{0},x^{1},x^{2},x^{3})
on
\mathbbm{R}^{1,3}
, where
x^{0}
represents time, and the shorthand notation
\partial_{\mu}
for the partial derivative
\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{\mu}}
. The standard Minkowski metric of signature
(+---)
is denoted
\eta_{\mu\nu}
, and the inner product of two vectors
v=(v^{\mu})
and
w=(w^{\mu})
in
\mathbbm{R}^{1,3}
is
v\cdot w=\eta_{\mu\nu}\,v^{\mu}\,w^{\nu}=v_{\mu}\,w^{\mu}
; unless otherwise explicitly stated, implicit summation over repeated indices is always understood throughout this paper. We write
v^{2}:=v\cdot v
. The standard volume form on
\mathbbm{R}^{1,3}
is

\displaystyle\mathrm{d}^{4}x=\mathrm{d}x^{0}\wedge\mathrm{d}x^{1}\wedge\mathrm{d}x^{2}\wedge\mathrm{d}x^{3}\ ,

(1.1)

and
\square=\eta^{\mu\nu}\,\partial_{\mu}\,\partial_{\nu}=\partial_{\mu}\,\partial^{\mu}
is the wave operator.
We denote by
\ast_{{\textrm{\tiny H}}}
the Hodge duality operator induced by the Minkowski metric
\eta_{\mu\nu}
.

We abbreviate momentum space integrals as

\displaystyle\int_{k,p,\dots}:=\int_{(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})^{*}}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}^{4}k}{(2\pi)^{4}}\ \int_{(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})^{*}}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}^{4}p}{(2\pi)^{4}}\ \cdots\ .

(1.2)

Throughout we use the formal representation

\displaystyle\int_{\mathbbm{R}^{1,3}}\,\mathrm{d}^{4}x\ \mathrm{e}^{\pm\,\mathrm{i}\,k\cdot x}=(2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(k)

(1.3)

of the Dirac distribution.

All vector spaces are defined over the ground field
\mathbbm{R}
of real numbers. For any vector space
V
and any integer
p\in\mathbbm{Z}
, elements of
V[p]
are of degree
-p
.

2
Classical Braided Scalar Electrodynamics

In this section we construct our novel model of braided scalar electrodynamics, starting from the well-known correspondence between perturbative classical field theories and
L_{\infty}
-algebras; see e.g.
[
28
,
25
]
for classic expository accounts.
The
L_{\infty}
-algebra formulation of ordinary scalar quantum electrodynamics with a Higgs potential appears in
[
29
,
30
]
, where spontaneous symmetry breaking and the Higgs mechanism are described using homotopy transfer.
The
L_{\infty}
-algebra description of the non-abelian version, i.e. scalar quantum chromodynamics, is considered by
[
31
]
in the context of tree-level scattering amplitudes and the perturbiner expansion in the corresponding minimal model.

2.1
Scalar Electrodynamics in the
L_{\infty}
-Algebra Formalism

We construct the cyclic
L_{\infty}
-algebra
\mathscr{L}=(L,\ell_{1},\ell_{2},\ell_{3},\langle-,-\rangle)
of classical scalar electrodynamics whose Maurer-Cartan functional is the standard action functional given by

\displaystyle{S}:=\int_{\mathbbm{R}^{1,3}}\,\mathrm{d}^{4}x\ D_{\mu}\bar{\phi}\,D^{\mu}\phi-m^{2}\,\bar{\phi}\,\phi-\frac{1}{4}\,F_{\mu\nu}\,F^{\mu\nu}\ .

(2.1)

The matter field is a complex scalar
\phi
of mass
m
which is minimally coupled to a
\mathsf{U}(1)
gauge field
A_{\mu}
through the covariant derivatives

\begin{split}D_{\mu}\phi&=\partial_{\mu}\phi-\mathrm{i}\,g\,A_{\mu}\,\phi\quad,\quad D_{\mu}\bar{\phi}=\partial_{\mu}\bar{\phi}+\mathrm{i}\,g\,\bar{\phi}\,A_{\mu}\ ,\end{split}

(2.2)

where
g
is the electromagnetic coupling constant.
The kinetic terms come with the field strength tensor

\displaystyle F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_{\mu}A_{\nu}-\partial_{\nu}A_{\mu}\ .

(2.3)

The action functional is invariant under infinitesimal gauge transformations with respect to a real parameter
c
, which are defined as

\begin{split}\delta_{c}\phi&=\mathrm{i}\,c\,\phi\quad,\quad\delta_{c}\bar{\phi}=-\mathrm{i}\,\bar{\phi}\,c\quad,\quad\delta_{c}A_{\mu}=\tfrac{1}{g}\,\partial_{\mu}c\ .\end{split}

(2.4)

The covariant derivatives satisfy
\delta_{c}(D_{\mu}\phi)=\mathrm{i}\,c\,D_{\mu}\phi
and similarly for their complex conjugates.

The graded vector space
L=L^{0}\oplus L^{1}\oplus L^{2}\oplus L^{3}
underlying the
L_{\infty}
-algebra
\mathscr{L}
has homogeneous components

\displaystyle L^{0}=L^{3}=\Omega^{0}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})\quad,\quad L^{1}=L^{2}=\Omega^{0}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})\oplus\Omega^{0}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})\oplus\Omega^{1}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})\ ,

(2.5)

which respectively organise the gauge symmetry, fields, equations of motion and Noether identities

c\ \in\ L^{0}\ ,\quad{\cal A}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\phi\\
\bar{\phi}\\
A\end{array}\right)\ \in\ L^{1}\ ,\quad\mathcal{A}^{+}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\bar{\phi}^{+}\\
\phi^{+}\\
A^{+}\end{array}\right)\ \in\ L^{2}\ ,\quad c^{+}\ \in\ L^{3}\ .

(2.6)

Here we used the isomorphism
\mathbbm{R}^{2}\simeq\mathbbm{C}
to identify
\Omega^{0}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})\oplus\Omega^{0}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})\simeq\Omega^{0}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})\otimes_{\mathbbm{R}}\mathbbm{C}
as the real vector spaces of complex scalar fields
(\phi,\bar{\phi}\,)
and
(\bar{\phi}^{+},\phi^{+})
, regarded as zero-forms on
\mathbbm{R}^{1,3}
. The gauge field
A
is regarded as a one-form and its field strength
F
as a two-form on
\mathbbm{R}^{1,3}
.

The complete list of non-zero
L_{\infty}
-brackets
\ell_{n}:\text{\Large$\wedge$}^{n}L\longrightarrow L[2-n]
is given by

\displaystyle\ell_{1}(c)

\displaystyle=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}0\\
0\\
\frac{1}{g}\,\partial_{\mu}c\end{array}\right)\ ,\quad\ell_{1}(\mathcal{A})=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}-(\square+m^{2})\,\bar{\phi}\\
-(\square+m^{2})\,\phi\\
\square A^{\mu}-\partial^{\mu}\,\partial_{\rho}A^{\rho}\end{array}\right)\ ,\quad\ell_{1}({\cal A}^{+})=\frac{1}{g}\,\partial_{\mu}A^{+\mu}\ ,

\displaystyle\ell_{2}(c,{\cal A})

\displaystyle=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\mathrm{i}\,c\,\phi\\
-\mathrm{i}\,\bar{\phi}\,c\\
0\end{array}\right)\ ,\quad\ell_{2}(c,\mathcal{A}^{+})=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\mathrm{i}\,c\,\bar{\phi}^{+}\\
-\mathrm{i}\,\phi^{+}\,c\\
0\end{array}\right)\ ,\quad\ell_{2}(c,c^{+})=0\ ,

\displaystyle\ell_{2}(\mathcal{A}_{1},\mathcal{A}_{2})

\displaystyle=\mathrm{i}\,g\,\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\bar{\phi}_{1}\,\partial_{\mu}A_{2}^{\mu}+\bar{\phi}_{2}\,\partial_{\mu}A_{1}^{\mu}+2\,\partial_{\mu}\bar{\phi}_{1}\,A_{2}^{\mu}+2\,\partial_{\mu}\bar{\phi}_{2}\,A_{1}^{\mu}\\[4.30554pt]
-\partial_{\mu}A_{1}^{\mu}\,\phi_{2}-\partial_{\mu}A_{2}^{\mu}\,\phi_{1}-2\,A_{1}^{\mu}\,\partial_{\mu}\phi_{2}-2\,A_{2}^{\mu}\,\partial_{\mu}\phi_{1}\\[4.30554pt]
\phi_{1}\,\partial^{\mu}\bar{\phi}_{2}+\phi_{2}\,\partial^{\mu}\bar{\phi}_{1}-\partial^{\mu}\phi_{1}\,\bar{\phi}_{2}-\partial^{\mu}\phi_{2}\,\bar{\phi}_{1}\end{array}\right)\ ,

\displaystyle\ell_{2}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A}^{+})

\displaystyle=-\mathrm{i}\,\phi^{+}\,\bar{\phi}+\mathrm{i}\,\bar{\phi}^{+}\,\phi\ ,

(2.7p)

\displaystyle\begin{split}&\ell_{3}(\mathcal{A}_{1},\mathcal{A}_{2},\mathcal{A}_{3})\\[4.0pt]
&\qquad=-g^{2}\,{\small\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\bar{\phi}_{1}\,A_{2\mu}\,A_{3}^{\mu}+\bar{\phi}_{2}\,A_{1\mu}\,A_{3}^{\mu}+\bar{\phi}_{1}\,A_{3\mu}\,A_{2}^{\mu}+\bar{\phi}_{3}\,A_{1\mu}\,A_{2}^{\mu}+\bar{\phi}_{2}\,A_{3\mu}\,A_{1}^{\mu}+\bar{\phi}_{3}\,A_{2\mu}\,A_{1}^{\mu}\\[3.87498pt]
A_{1\mu}\,A_{2}^{\mu}\,\phi_{3}+A_{2\mu}\,A_{1}^{\mu}\,\phi_{3}+A_{1\mu}\,A_{3}^{\mu}\,\phi_{2}+A_{3\mu}\,A_{1}^{\mu}\,\phi_{2}+A_{2\mu}\,A_{3}^{\mu}\,\phi_{1}+A_{3\mu}\,A_{2}^{\mu}\,\phi_{1}\\[3.87498pt]
2\,\big(\phi_{1}\,\bar{\phi}_{2}\,A_{3}^{\mu}+\phi_{2}\,\bar{\phi}_{1}\,A_{3}^{\mu}+\phi_{1}\,\bar{\phi}_{3}\,A_{2}^{\mu}+\phi_{2}\,\bar{\phi}_{3}\,A_{1}^{\mu}+\phi_{3}\,\bar{\phi}_{1}\,A_{2}^{\mu}+\phi_{3}\,\bar{\phi}_{2}\,A_{1}^{\mu}\big)\end{array}\right)}\normalsize\ .\end{split}

(2.7q)

The cyclic inner product
\langle-,-\rangle:L\otimes L\longrightarrow\mathbbm{R}[-3]
is defined by

\displaystyle\begin{split}\langle c,c^{+}\rangle=\int_{\mathbbm{R}^{1,3}}\,c\ast_{\textrm{\tiny H}}c^{+}\quad,\quad\langle{\cal A},\mathcal{A}^{+}\rangle=\int_{\mathbbm{R}^{1,3}}\,A\wedge\ast_{\textrm{\tiny H}}\,{A}^{+}+\bar{\phi}^{+}\ast_{\textrm{\tiny H}}\phi+\bar{\phi}\ast_{\textrm{\tiny H}}\phi^{+}\ .\end{split}

(2.8)

Using these brackets and pairing one easily checks that the Maurer-Cartan functional

\displaystyle\mathcal{S}(\mathscr{L}):=\tfrac{1}{2!}\,\langle\mathcal{A},\ell_{1}(\mathcal{A})\rangle-\tfrac{1}{3!}\,\langle\mathcal{A},\ell_{2}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A})\rangle-\tfrac{1}{4!}\,\langle\mathcal{A},\ell_{3}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A})\rangle

(2.9)

reproduces the classical action functional (
2.1
) of scalar electrodynamics:
\mathcal{S}(\mathscr{L})=S
.

Maurer-Cartan theory also recovers the curvature
\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}}\in L^{2}
of the generalized gauge field
\mathcal{A}\in L^{1}
given by

\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}}:=\ell_{1}(\mathcal{A})-\tfrac{1}{2!}\,\ell_{2}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A})-\tfrac{1}{3!}\,\ell_{3}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A})\ .

(2.10)

It is covariant under gauge variations
\delta_{c}\mathcal{A}=\ell_{1}(c)+\ell_{2}(c,\mathcal{A})
, i.e.
\delta_{c}\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}}=\ell_{2}(c,\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}})
, and its components read explicitly

\begin{split}\mathcal{F}_{\phi}&=-(\square+m^{2})\,\bar{\phi}-\mathrm{i}\,g\,\partial_{\mu}(\bar{\phi}\,A^{\mu})-\mathrm{i}\,g\,\partial_{\mu}\bar{\phi}\,A^{\mu}+g^{2}\,\bar{\phi}\,A_{\mu}\,A^{\mu}\ ,\\[4.0pt]
\mathcal{F}_{\bar{\phi}}&=-(\square+m^{2})\,\phi+\mathrm{i}\,g\,\partial_{\mu}(A^{\mu}\,\phi)+\mathrm{i}\,g\,A^{\mu}\,\partial_{\mu}\phi+g^{2}\,A_{\mu}\,A^{\mu}\,\phi\ ,\\[4.0pt]
\mathcal{F}_{A}^{\mu}&=\square A^{\mu}-\partial^{\mu}\,\partial_{\nu}A^{\nu}+\mathrm{i}\,g\,\partial^{\mu}\phi\,\bar{\phi}-\mathrm{i}\,g\,\phi\,\partial^{\mu}\bar{\phi}+2\,g^{2}\,\phi\,\bar{\phi}\,A^{\mu}\ .\end{split}

(2.11)

The Maurer-Cartan equations
\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}}=0
define the space of classical solutions
\mathcal{A}
to the field equations of scalar electrodynamics.

The Noether identity for the
\mathsf{U}(1)
gauge symmetry
\delta_{c}\mathcal{A}=\ell_{1}(c)+\ell_{2}(c,\mathcal{A})
is encoded in Maurer-Cartan theory by the off-shell Bianchi identity in
L^{3}
for the curvature
\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}}
given by

\begin{split}\mathsf{d}_{\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}}:=\ell_{1}(\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}})+\ell_{2}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}})=\tfrac{1}{g}\,\partial_{\mu}\mathcal{F}_{A}^{\mu}+\mathrm{i}\,\bar{\phi}\,\mathcal{F}_{\bar{\phi}}-\mathrm{i}\,\mathcal{F}_{\phi}\,\phi\ =\ 0\ .\end{split}

(2.12)

After putting the photon on-shell,
\mathcal{F}_{A}^{\mu}=0
, this identity implies that

J_{\mu}:=\mathrm{i}\,\big(\phi\,D_{\mu}\bar{\phi}-D_{\mu}\phi\,\bar{\phi}\,\big)

(2.13)

is the weakly conserved Noether current for the global
\mathsf{U}(1)
symmetry of the complex scalar field from (
2.4
), i.e.
\partial_{\mu}J^{\mu}\approx 0
, where
\approx
indicates a weak equality that holds only up to equations of motion. It minimally couples to the gauge field
A_{\mu}
in the action functional (
2.1
).

2.2
Minimal Model of Scalar Electrodynamics

The differential
\ell_{1}
from (
2.7
) defines the underlying cochain complex
\mathsf{Ch}(\mathscr{L})=(L,\ell_{1})
of the
L_{\infty}
-algebra
\mathscr{L}
of scalar electrodynamics. It reads explicitly

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega^{0}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})\!\!}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\!\!\Omega^{1}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})[-1]\!\!}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\!\!\Omega^{1}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})[-2]\!\!}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\!\!\Omega^{0}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})[-3]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\oplus}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\oplus}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{matrix}\Omega^{0}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})[-1]\\[3.87498pt]
\oplus\\[3.87498pt]
\Omega^{0}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})[-1]\end{matrix}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{matrix}\Omega^{0}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})[-2]\\[3.87498pt]
\oplus\\[3.87498pt]
\Omega^{0}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})[-2]\end{matrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\frac{1}{g}\,\mathrm{d}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{d}^{\dagger}\,\mathrm{d}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\frac{1}{g}\,\mathrm{d}^{\dagger}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ {\ \ \Big(\begin{matrix}0\!\!&\!\!-\square-m^{2}\\[-0.81375pt]
-\square-m^{2}\!\!&\!\!0\end{matrix}\Big)\ }\ \ }

(2.14)

where
\mathrm{d}
is the exterior differential and
\mathrm{d}^{\dagger}:=\ast_{{\textrm{\tiny H}}}\,\mathrm{d}\,\ast_{{\textrm{\tiny H}}}
is the codifferential.

The cohomology of this complex defines a cyclic
L_{\infty}
-algebra
H^{\bullet}(\mathscr{L})
quasi-isomorphic to
\mathscr{L}
with underlying cochain complex
\mathsf{Ch}\big(H^{\bullet}(\mathscr{L})\big)=\big(H^{\bullet}({L}),0\big)
, called the minimal model for the
L_{\infty}
-algebra
\mathscr{L}

[
25
,
31
]
.
It describes the free field theory, or equivalently the linearized Maurer-Cartan equations.
In particular, fields
(A^{\textrm{\tiny(0)}},\phi^{\textrm{\tiny(0)}},\bar{\phi}{}^{\textrm{\tiny(0)}})
in the degree
1
cohomology

\displaystyle H^{1}({L})=\frac{\ker(\mathrm{d}^{\dagger}\,\mathrm{d})}{{\rm im}(\mathrm{d})}\ \oplus\ \ker\bigg(\begin{matrix}0&-\square-m^{2}\,\\
-\square-m^{2}&0\end{matrix}\bigg)

(2.15)

correspond to the usual plane wave photon states
A^{\textrm{\tiny(0)}}
of Maxwell theory on
\mathbbm{R}^{1,3}
and the conventional description of a free massive complex scalar as states
(\phi^{\textrm{\tiny(0)}},\bar{\phi}{}^{\textrm{\tiny(0)}})
satisfying the Klein-Gordon equation.

At the level of cochain complexes, scalar electrodynamics and its minimal model fit into the homotopy equivalence data of a deformation retract

}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-10.40335pt}{-9.6722pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform=matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -14.4 -13.38)} \pgfsys@hbox{58}\lxSVG@closescope }}}

\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\ ,

(2.16)

where
p\circ\iota=\mathrm{id}_{H^{\bullet}({L})}
and the map
\iota\circ p
decomposes into

\iota\circ p=\mathrm{id}_{{L}}+\ell_{1}\circ\mathsf{h}+\mathsf{h}\circ\ell_{1}\ .

(2.17)

The homogeneous components of the contracting homotopy
\mathsf{h}:L\longrightarrow{L}[-1]
are denoted by
\mathsf{h}^{{\textrm{\tiny(k)}}}:L^{k}\longrightarrow L^{k-1}
. The degree
2
component
\mathsf{h}^{{\textrm{\tiny(2)}}}=-\mathsf{G}_{\scriptscriptstyle\textrm{F}}:L^{2}\longrightarrow L^{1}
is given by the Feynman propagators
\mathsf{G}_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm F}
of scalar electrodynamics, which satisfy
\mathsf{G}_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm F}\circ\ell_{1}=\mathrm{id}_{L^{1}}
and
\ell_{1}\circ\mathsf{G}_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm F}=\mathrm{id}_{L^{2}}
on triplets of fields.

The contracting homotopy
\mathsf{h}
is not unique. A convenient choice is obtained starting from the massive scalar Feynman propagator, which is the degree 0 map
\mathsf{G}:\Omega^{0}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})\longrightarrow\Omega^{0}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})
given by

\mathsf{G}=-\frac{1}{\square+m^{2}}\quad,\quad\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(k)=\frac{1}{k^{2}-m^{2}}\ .

(2.18)

In the second expression we wrote the momentum space representation, i.e. the eigenvalues of
\mathsf{G}
when acting on plane wave eigenfunctions of the form
\mathrm{e}^{\pm\,\mathrm{i}\,k\cdot x}
. These should be understood throughout as defined using the standard Feynman
\mathrm{i}\,\epsilon
-prescription, but for brevity we do not write it explicitly.

Similarly, the massless scalar Feynman propagator
\mathsf{D}:\Omega^{0}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})\longrightarrow\Omega^{0}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})
is given by

\mathsf{D}=\frac{1}{\square}\ \quad,\quad\mathsf{\tilde{D}}(k)=-\frac{1}{k^{2}}\ .

(2.19)

We extend this to a map
\mathsf{D}:\Omega^{1}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})\longrightarrow\Omega^{1}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})
using the
\Omega^{0}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})
-module structure of the vector space of one-forms.
Finally, introduce the projector
\mathsf{\Pi}:\Omega^{1}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})\longrightarrow\Omega^{1}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})
onto the image of the Maxwell operator
\mathrm{d}^{\dagger}\,\mathrm{d}
, with matrix elements

\begin{split}\mathsf{\Pi}_{\mu\nu}=\eta_{\mu\nu}-\frac{\partial_{\mu}\,\partial_{\nu}}{\square}\quad,\quad\tilde{\mathsf{\Pi}}_{\mu\nu}(k)=\eta_{\mu\nu}-\frac{k_{\mu}\,k_{\nu}}{k^{2}}\ .\end{split}

(2.20)

Then the components of the contracting homotopy satisfying (
2.17
) are given by

\begin{split}\mathsf{h}^{{\textrm{\tiny(1)}}}(\mathcal{A})=-g\,\mathsf{D}\,\mathrm{d}^{\dagger}A\quad,\quad\mathsf{h}^{{\textrm{\tiny(2)}}}(\mathcal{A}^{+})=-\begin{pmatrix}\mathsf{G}\,\phi^{+}\\
\mathsf{G}\,\bar{\phi}^{+}\\
\mathsf{D}\,{\mathsf{\Pi}}\,A^{+}\end{pmatrix}\quad,\quad\mathsf{h}^{{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}}(c^{+})=-g\begin{pmatrix}0\\
0\\
\mathsf{D}\,\mathrm{d}\,c^{+}\end{pmatrix}\ .\end{split}

(2.21)

In terms of coordinate functions

\begin{split}\mathsf{h}^{{\textrm{\tiny(1)}}}(A_{\mu})=-g\,\frac{\partial^{\mu}}{\square}A_{\mu}\ ,\ \mathsf{h}^{{\textrm{\tiny(2)}}}\begin{pmatrix}\bar{\phi}^{+}\\
\phi^{+}\\
A^{+\mu}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\displaystyle\frac{1}{\square+m^{2}}\,\phi^{+}\\[8.61108pt]
\displaystyle\frac{1}{\square+m^{2}}\,\bar{\phi}^{+}\\[8.61108pt]
\displaystyle-\frac{1}{\square}\,\Big(\delta^{\mu}_{\nu}-\frac{\partial^{\mu}\,\partial_{\nu}}{\square}\Big)\,A^{+\nu}\end{pmatrix}\ ,\ \mathsf{h}^{{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}}(c^{+})&=-g\,\frac{\partial_{\mu}}{\square}\,c^{+}\ .\end{split}

(2.22)

Gauge fixing is performed by enforcing
A\in\mathrm{ker}(\mathsf{h}^{{\textrm{\tiny(1)}}})
. The choice of contracting homotopy above with
\mathsf{h}^{{\textrm{\tiny(1)}}}:\Omega^{1}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})\longrightarrow\Omega^{0}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})
defines the Lorenz gauge.

2.3
Scalar Electrodynamics in the Braided
L_{\infty}
-Algebra Formalism

We will now deform the cyclic
L_{\infty}
-algebra of scalar electrodynamics from
section

2.1
into a cyclic braided
L_{\infty}
-algebra
\mathscr{L}^{\star}=(L,\ell_{1}^{\star},\ell_{2}^{\star},\ell_{3}^{\star},\langle-,-\rangle_{\star})
, according to the formalism introduced in
[
1
,
2
]
. The underlying graded vector space
L
is unchanged, while the structure maps of
\mathscr{L}^{\star}
are deformed according to Drinfel’d twist deformation quantization. The Maurer-Cartan theory for the cyclic braided
L_{\infty}
-algebra
\mathscr{L}^{\star}
defines a new noncommutative deformation of the theory from
section

2.1
, which we call
braided scalar electrodynamics
. We describe its gauge symmetries and dynamics following
[
1
,
2
]
.

Drinfel’d Twist Deformation.

As in
[
6
]
, in this paper we focus on the translation symmetries of scalar electrodynamics and work with the abelian Moyal-Weyl twist

\begin{split}\mathcal{F}=\exp\left(-\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2}\,\theta^{\mu\nu}\,{\pounds}_{\mu}\otimes{\pounds}_{\nu}\right)\ ,\end{split}

(2.23)

where
\theta
is a constant bivector on
\mathbbm{R}^{1,3}
and
\pounds_{\mu}:=\pounds_{\partial_{\mu}}
are Lie derivatives along the holonomic frame of vector fields on
\mathbbm{R}^{1,3}
. The operator (
2.23
) acts on tensor products (over
\mathbbm{C}
) of spaces of classical tensor fields (over
\Omega^{0}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})
).

If
\mu:\mathcal{T}\otimes\mathcal{T}\longrightarrow\mathcal{T}
is a binary operation on a tensor space
\mathcal{T}
, then the twist (
2.23
) can be used to deform it into another binary operation

\displaystyle\mu_{\star}:=\mu\circ\mathcal{F}^{-1}\ .

(2.24)

This preserves associativity properties of the operation
\mu
, but it generally deforms any commutativity properties to
braided
commutativity. For example, if
\mu(T_{1}\otimes T_{2})=\mu(T_{2}\otimes T_{1})
for
T_{1},T_{2}\in\mathcal{T}
, then

\displaystyle\mu_{\star}(T_{1}\otimes T_{2})=\mu_{\star}\circ{\mathcal{R}}^{-1}(T_{2}\otimes T_{1})=\mu_{\star}\big(\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(T_{2})\otimes\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(T_{1})\big)\ ,

(2.25)

where

\displaystyle{\mathcal{R}}=\mathcal{F}^{-2}

(2.26)

is the universal
R
-matrix and we use the standard notation
{\mathcal{R}}^{-1}=\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}\otimes\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}
(with summation understood). This deformation naturally extends to higher
n
-ary operations as well as to more general maps among combinations of different tensor spaces.

The Cyclic Braided
{\boldsymbol{L_{\infty}}}
-Algebra
{\mathscr{L}^{\star}}
.

Running the Drinfel’d twist machine on the brackets of
section

2.1
, the non-zero brackets
\ell_{n}^{\star}:\text{\Large$\wedge$}^{n}L\longrightarrow L[2-n]
of the braided
L_{\infty}
-algebra
\mathscr{L}^{\star}
are given by

\displaystyle\ell_{1}^{\star}(c)

\displaystyle=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}0\\
0\\
\frac{1}{g}\,\partial_{\mu}c\end{array}\right)\quad,\quad\ell_{1}^{\star}({\cal A})=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}-(\square+m^{2})\,\bar{\phi}\\
-(\square+m^{2})\,\phi\\
\square A^{\mu}-\partial^{\mu}\,\partial_{\rho}A^{\rho}\end{array}\right)\quad,\quad\ell_{1}^{\star}(\mathcal{A}^{+})=\frac{1}{g}\,\partial_{\mu}A^{+\mu}\ ,

\displaystyle\small\ell^{\star}_{2}(c,{\cal A})

\displaystyle={\small\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\mathrm{i}\,c\star\phi\\
-\mathrm{i}\,\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(\bar{\phi})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(c)\\
0\end{array}\right)}\normalsize\ ,\ \ell^{\star}_{2}(c,\mathcal{A}^{+})={\small\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\mathrm{i}\,\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(\bar{\phi}^{+})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(c)\\
-\mathrm{i}\,c\star\phi^{+}\\
0\end{array}\right)}\normalsize\ ,\ \ell^{\star}_{2}(c,c^{+})=0\ ,\normalsize

\displaystyle\ell_{2}^{\star}(\mathcal{A}_{1},\mathcal{A}_{2})

\displaystyle=\mathrm{i}\,g\,{\small\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\bar{\phi}_{1}\star\partial_{\mu}A_{2}^{\mu}+\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(\bar{\phi}_{2})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(\partial_{\mu}A_{1}^{\mu})+2\,\partial_{\mu}\bar{\phi}_{1}\star A_{2}^{\mu}+2\,\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(\partial_{\mu}\bar{\phi}_{2})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(A_{1}^{\mu})\\[3.87498pt]
-\partial_{\mu}A_{1}^{\mu}\star\phi_{2}-\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(\partial_{\mu}A_{2}^{\mu})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(\phi_{1})-2\,A_{1}^{\mu}\star\partial_{\mu}\phi_{2}-2\,\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(A_{2}^{\mu})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(\partial_{\mu}\phi_{1})\\[3.87498pt]
\phi_{1}\star\partial^{\mu}\bar{\phi}_{2}+\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(\phi_{2})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(\partial^{\mu}\bar{\phi}_{1})-\partial^{\mu}\phi_{1}\star\bar{\phi}_{2}-\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(\partial^{\mu}\phi_{2})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(\bar{\phi}_{1})\end{array}\right)}\normalsize\ ,

\displaystyle\ell_{2}^{\star}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A}^{+})

\displaystyle=-\mathrm{i}\,\bar{\phi}\star\phi^{+}+\mathrm{i}\,\phi\star\bar{\phi}^{+}\ ,

(2.27p)

\displaystyle\ell_{3}^{\star}(\mathcal{A}_{1},\mathcal{A}_{2},\mathcal{A}_{3})=-g^{2}\,{\small\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\bar{\phi}_{1}\star A_{2\mu}\star A_{3}^{\mu}+\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(\bar{\phi}_{2})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(A_{1\mu})\star A_{3}^{\mu}\\[3.87498pt]
+\,\bar{\phi}_{1}\star\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(A_{3\mu})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(A_{2}^{\mu})+\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(\bar{\phi}_{3})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(A_{1\mu}\star A_{2}^{\mu})\\[3.87498pt]
+\,\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(\bar{\phi}_{2}\star A_{3\mu})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(A_{1}^{\mu})+\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(\bar{\phi}_{3})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(\mathsf{R}_{\beta}(A_{2\mu})\star\mathsf{R}^{\beta}(A_{1}^{\mu}))\\
\\
A_{1\mu}\star A_{2}^{\mu}\star\phi_{3}+\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(A_{2\mu})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(A_{1}^{\mu})\star\phi_{3}\\[3.87498pt]
+\,A_{1\mu}\star\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(A_{3}^{\mu})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(\phi_{2})+\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(A_{3\mu})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(A_{1}^{\mu}\star\phi_{2})\\[3.87498pt]
+\,\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(A_{2\mu}\star A_{3}^{\mu})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(\phi_{1})+\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(A_{3\mu})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(\mathsf{R}_{\beta}(A_{2}^{\mu})\star\mathsf{R}^{\beta}(\phi_{1}))\\
\\
2\,\big[\phi_{1}\star\bar{\phi}_{2}\star A_{3}^{\mu}+\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(\phi_{2})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(\bar{\phi}_{1})\star A_{3}^{\mu}\\[3.87498pt]
+\,\phi_{1}\star\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(\bar{\phi}_{3})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(A_{2}^{\mu})+\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(\phi_{3})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(\bar{\phi}_{1}\star A_{2}^{\mu})\\[3.87498pt]
+\,\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(\phi_{2}\star\bar{\phi}_{3})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(A_{1}^{\mu})+\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(\phi_{3})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(\mathsf{R}_{\beta}(\bar{\phi}_{2})\star\mathsf{R}^{\beta}(A_{1}^{\mu}))\big]\end{array}\right)}\normalsize\ .

The Moyal-Weyl twist deformation of the cyclic inner product (
2.8
) yields a pairing for
\mathscr{L}^{\star}
which is strictly cyclic. It is given explicitly by

\displaystyle\begin{split}\langle c,c^{+}\rangle_{\star}=\int_{\mathbbm{R}^{3,1}}\,c\wedge_{\star}\ast_{\textrm{\tiny H}}\,c^{+}\ ,\ \langle{\cal A},\mathcal{A}^{+}\rangle_{\star}=\int_{\mathbbm{R}^{1,3}}\,A\wedge_{\star}\ast_{\textrm{\tiny H}}\,A^{+}+\bar{\phi}^{+}\wedge_{\star}\ast_{\textrm{\tiny H}}\,\phi+\bar{\phi}\wedge_{\star}\ast_{\textrm{\tiny H}}\,\phi^{+}\ .\end{split}

(2.28)

Braided Gauge Symmetry.

The (left) braided gauge transformations by
c\in L^{0}
are given by
[
1
,
2
]

\delta_{c}^{\star}\mathcal{A}=\ell_{1}^{\star}(c)+\ell_{2}^{\star}(c,\mathcal{A})
, which read explicitly

\begin{split}\delta^{\star}_{c}\phi=\mathrm{i}\,c\star\phi\quad,\quad\delta^{\star}_{c}\bar{\phi}=-\mathrm{i}\,\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(\bar{\phi})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(c)\quad,\quad\delta^{\star}_{c}A_{\mu}=\tfrac{1}{g}\,\partial_{\mu}c\ .\end{split}

(2.29)

The gauge variations close a trivial braided commutator algebra

\displaystyle[\delta^{\star}_{c_{1}},\delta^{\star}_{c_{2}}]^{\star}:=\delta_{c_{1}}^{\star}\circ\delta_{c_{2}}^{\star}-\delta_{\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(c_{2})}^{\star}\circ\delta_{\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(c_{1})}^{\star}=0\ ,

(2.30)

reflecting the abelian nature of the braided
\mathsf{U}(1)
gauge symmetry, or equivalently the vanishing brackets
\ell_{2}^{\star}(c_{1},c_{2})=0
.

Maurer-Cartan Equations.

The braided curvature
\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\star}\in L^{2}
of a generalized gauge field
\mathcal{A}\in L^{1}
obtained from Maurer-Cartan theory is given by the formula (
2.10
) applied to the braided brackets in (
2.27
). It is covariant under braided gauge variations, i.e.
\delta_{c}^{\star}\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\star}=\ell_{2}^{\star}(c,\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\star})
, and its components are given explicitly by

\begin{split}\mathcal{F}_{\phi}^{\star}&=-(\square+m^{2})\,\bar{\phi}-\tfrac{\mathrm{i}\,g}{2}\,\big(\bar{\phi}\star\partial_{\mu}A^{\mu}+\partial_{\mu}A^{\mu}\star\bar{\phi}+2\,\partial_{\mu}\bar{\phi}\star A^{\mu}+2\,A^{\mu}\star\partial_{\mu}\bar{\phi}\big)\\
&\hskip 56.9055pt+\tfrac{g^{2}}{3}\,\big(\bar{\phi}\star A_{\mu}\star A^{\mu}+A_{\mu}\star\bar{\phi}\star A^{\mu}+A_{\mu}\star A^{\mu}\star\bar{\phi}\big)\ ,\\[4.0pt]
\mathcal{F}_{\bar{\phi}}^{\star}&=-(\square+m^{2})\,\phi+\tfrac{\mathrm{i}\,g}{2}\,\big(\partial_{\mu}A^{\mu}\star\phi+\phi\star\partial_{\mu}A^{\mu}+2\,A^{\mu}\star\partial_{\mu}\phi+2\,\partial_{\mu}\phi\star A^{\mu}\big)\\
&\hskip 56.9055pt+\tfrac{g^{2}}{3}\,\big(A_{\mu}\star A^{\mu}\star\phi+A_{\mu}\star\phi\star A^{\mu}+\phi\star A_{\mu}\star A^{\mu}\big)\ ,\\[4.0pt]
\mathcal{F}^{\star\mu}_{A}&=\square A^{\mu}-\partial^{\mu}\,\partial_{\nu}A^{\nu}+\tfrac{\mathrm{i}\,g}{2}\,\big(\partial^{\mu}\phi\star\bar{\phi}+\bar{\phi}\star\partial^{\mu}\phi-\phi\star\partial^{\mu}\bar{\phi}-\partial^{\mu}\bar{\phi}\star\phi\big)\\
&\hskip 56.9055pt+\tfrac{g^{2}}{3}\,\big(\phi\star\bar{\phi}\star A^{\mu}+\bar{\phi}\star\phi\star A^{\mu}+\phi\star A^{\mu}\star\bar{\phi}\\
&\hskip 113.81102pt+\bar{\phi}\star A^{\mu}\star\phi+A^{\mu}\star\phi\star\bar{\phi}+A^{\mu}\star\bar{\phi}\star\phi\big)\ .\end{split}

(2.31)

The Maurer-Cartan equations
\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\star}=0
define the equations of motion for the scalar and gauge fields.
We can rewrite them in a more compact form by defining left and right covariant derivatives

D_{\mu}^{\mbox{\tiny L}}\phi=\partial_{\mu}\phi-\mathrm{i}\,g\,A_{\mu}\star\phi\quad,\quad D_{\mu}^{\mbox{\tiny R}}\phi=\partial_{\mu}\phi-\mathrm{i}\,g\,\phi\star A_{\mu}=\partial_{\mu}\phi-\mathrm{i}\,g\,\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(A_{\mu})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(\phi)\ .

(2.32)

They are braided gauge covariant, i.e.
\delta_{c}^{\star}(D^{\mbox{\tiny L,R}}_{\mu}\phi)=\mathrm{i}\,c\star D_{\mu}^{\mbox{\tiny L,R}}\phi
, and similarly for their complex conjugates. In the commutative limit
\theta=0
, they both reduce to the covariant derivatives introduced in (
2.2
).
With them we present the equations of motion for braided scalar electrodynamics as

\displaystyle\begin{split}&\tfrac{1}{2}\,D_{\mu}^{\mbox{\tiny L}\,}D^{{\mbox{\tiny L}}\mu}\phi+\tfrac{1}{2}\,D_{\mu}^{\mbox{\tiny R}}\,D^{{\mbox{\tiny R}}\mu}\phi+m^{2}\,\phi+\tfrac{g^{2}}{6}\,\big(A_{\mu}\star A^{\mu}\star\phi+\phi\star A_{\mu}\star A^{\mu}-2\,A^{\mu}\star\phi\star A_{\mu}\big)\ =\ 0\ ,\\[4.0pt]
&\partial_{\rho}F^{\rho\mu}-\tfrac{\mathrm{i}\,g}{4}\,\big[\phi\star(D^{{\mbox{\tiny L}}\mu}\bar{\phi}+D^{{\mbox{\tiny R}}\mu}\bar{\phi})+(D^{{\mbox{\tiny L}}\mu}\bar{\phi}+D^{{\mbox{\tiny R}}\mu}\bar{\phi})\star\phi\\
&\hskip 71.13188pt-\bar{\phi}\star(D^{{\mbox{\tiny L}}\mu}\phi+D^{{\mbox{\tiny R}}\mu}\phi)-(D^{{\mbox{\tiny L}}\mu}\phi+D^{{\mbox{\tiny R}}\mu}\phi)\star\bar{\phi}\big]\\
&\hskip 113.81102pt+\tfrac{g^{2}}{12}\,\big(\phi\star\bar{\phi}\star A^{\mu}+\bar{\phi}\star\phi\star A^{\mu}+A^{\mu}\star\phi\star\bar{\phi}+A^{\mu}\star\bar{\phi}\star\phi\\
&\hskip 156.49014pt-2\,\phi\star A^{\mu}\star\bar{\phi}-2\,\bar{\phi}\star A^{\mu}\star\phi\big)\ =\ 0\ .\end{split}

(2.33)

We stress that here the classical field strength (
2.3
) is invariant:
\delta_{c}^{\star}F_{\mu\nu}=0
. Despite the lack of manifest braided gauge covariance of the individual cubic terms proportional to
g^{2}
in (
2.33
), their overall combinations are covariant. This is guaranteed by covariance of the braided curvature, and can also be checked by explicit calculation. This is a typical feature of gauge theories whose braided
L_{\infty}
-algebras involve higher brackets and thus do not define differential graded braided Lie algebras
[
1
,
2
]
. In the commutative limit
\theta=0
, the individual non-covariant terms cancel each other and we recover the equations of motion of scalar electrodynamics from
section

2.1
.

Braided Noether Identity.

Braided field theories differ most profoundly from ordinary field theories and noncommutative field theories with star-gauge symmetry through their braided gauge symmetries. This is dually reflected in their realisations of the corresponding Noether identities
[
1
,
2
]
. The braided Noether identity is a Bianchi identity for the braided curvature
\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\star}
resulting from the homotopy Jacobi identities for the braided
L_{\infty}
-algebra
\mathscr{L}^{\star}
in
L^{3}
. In the present case it reduces to

\begin{split}\mathsf{d}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\star}\mathcal{F}^{\star}_{\mathcal{A}}&:=\ell_{1}^{\star}(\mathcal{F}^{\star}_{\mathcal{A}})+\tfrac{1}{2!}\,\big(\ell_{2}^{\star}(\mathcal{F}^{\star}_{\mathcal{A}},\mathcal{A})-\ell_{2}^{\star}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{F}^{\star}_{\mathcal{A}})\big)+\tfrac{1}{3!}\,\ell_{1}^{\star}\big(\ell^{\star}_{3}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A})\big)\\
&\hskip 56.9055pt+\tfrac{1}{2\cdot 2!}\,\big(\ell_{2}^{\star}(\ell_{2}^{\star}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A}),\mathcal{A})-\ell_{2}^{\star}(\mathcal{A},\ell_{2}^{\star}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A}))\big)\\
&\hskip 113.81102pt+\tfrac{1}{2\cdot 3!}\,\big(\ell_{2}^{\star}(\ell_{3}^{\star}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A}),\mathcal{A}))-\ell_{2}^{\star}(\mathcal{A},\ell_{3}^{\star}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A}))\big)\ =\ 0\ .\end{split}

(2.34)

After expanding out the curvature in brackets, most terms cancel, leaving

\begin{split}\ell_{1}^{\star}(\mathcal{F}^{\star}_{\mathcal{A}})+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\big(\ell_{2}^{\star}(\ell_{1}^{\star}(\mathcal{A}),\mathcal{A})-\ell_{2}^{\star}(\mathcal{A},\ell_{1}^{\star}(\mathcal{A}))\big)+\tfrac{1}{6}\,\ell_{1}^{\star}\big(\ell_{3}^{\star}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A})\big)\ =\ 0\ .\end{split}

(2.35)

This leads to the braided analogue of (
2.12
) given by

\begin{split}\tfrac{1}{g}\,\partial_{\mu}\mathcal{F}^{\star\mu}_{A}+\partial_{\mu}J^{\star\mu}\ =\ 0\ ,\end{split}

(2.36)

where

\begin{split}J_{\mu}^{\star}&=\tfrac{\mathrm{i}}{2}\,\big(\partial_{\mu}\phi\star\bar{\phi}+\bar{\phi}\star\partial_{\mu}\phi-\phi\star\partial_{\mu}\bar{\phi}-\partial_{\mu}\bar{\phi}\star\phi\big)\\
&\quad\,+\tfrac{g}{3}\,\big(\phi\star\bar{\phi}\star A_{\mu}+\bar{\phi}\star\phi\star A_{\mu}+\phi\star A_{\mu}\star\bar{\phi}+\bar{\phi}\star A_{\mu}\star\phi+A_{\mu}\star\phi\star\bar{\phi}+A_{\mu}\star\bar{\phi}\star\phi\big)\ .\end{split}

(2.37)

Using the covariant derivatives (
2.32
), the one-form (
2.37
) can be brought to the covariant form

\begin{split}&J^{\star}_{\mu}:=\tfrac{\mathrm{i}}{4}\,\big(\phi\star(D^{\mbox{\tiny L}}_{\mu}\bar{\phi}+D^{\mbox{\tiny R}}_{\mu}\bar{\phi})-(D^{\mbox{\tiny L}}_{\mu}\phi+D_{\mu}^{\mbox{\tiny R}}\phi)\star\bar{\phi}\\
&\hskip 56.9055pt+(D_{\mu}^{\mbox{\tiny L}}\bar{\phi}+D_{\mu}^{\mbox{\tiny R}}\bar{\phi})\star\phi-\bar{\phi}\star(D_{\mu}^{\mbox{\tiny L}}\phi+D_{\mu}^{\mbox{\tiny R}}\phi)\big)\\
&\hskip 85.35826pt-\tfrac{g}{12}\,\big(\phi\star\bar{\phi}\star A_{\mu}+A_{\mu}\star\phi\star\bar{\phi}+\bar{\phi}\star\phi\star A_{\mu}+A_{\mu}\star\bar{\phi}\star\phi\\
&\hskip 142.26378pt-2\,\phi\star A_{\mu}\star\bar{\phi}-2\,\bar{\phi}\star A_{\mu}\star\phi\big)\ .\end{split}

(2.38)

By putting the photon on-shell,
\mathcal{F}_{A}^{\star\mu}=0
, this defines a new weakly conserved braided electric current
J^{\star}\in\Omega^{1}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})
analogously to the commutative case. Again despite the manifestly non-covariant individual cubic terms proportional to
g
in (
2.38
), it is a gauge invariant quantity. This current reduces to (
2.13
) in the commutative limit
\theta=0
. In general, however, the braided
\mathsf{U}(1)
charge conservation is vastly different from the usual case, see
[
6
]
.

Maurer-Cartan Functional.

The action functional for braided scalar electrodynamics is obtained using the formula (
2.9
) from Maurer-Cartan theory applied to the braided brackets in (
2.27
) and the cyclic inner product in (
2.28
). It is given explicitly by

\begin{split}S_{\star}:=\mathcal{S}(\mathscr{L}^{\star})&=\int_{\mathbbm{R}^{1,3}}\,{\rm d}^{4}x\ \bigg(\,\frac{1}{4}\,\big(D_{\mu}^{\mbox{\tiny L}}\bar{\phi}+D_{\mu}^{\mbox{\tiny R}}\bar{\phi}\big)\star\big(D^{{\mbox{\tiny L}}\mu}\phi+D^{{\mbox{\tiny R}}\mu}\phi\big)-m^{2}\,\bar{\phi}\star\phi-\frac{1}{4}\,F_{\mu\nu}\star F^{\mu\nu}\\
&\hskip 85.35826pt+\frac{g^{2}}{12}\,\bar{\phi}\star\big(A_{\mu}\star A^{\mu}\star\phi+\phi\star A_{\mu}\star A^{\mu}-2\,A^{\mu}\star\phi\star A_{\mu}\big)\bigg)\ .\end{split}

(2.39)

It is invariant under braided gauge transformations and reduces to (
2.1
) in the commutative limit.

Minimal Model.

For any braided field theory
[
1
,
2
]
, the underlying cochain complex
\mathsf{Ch}(\mathscr{L}^{\star})
coincides with the cochain complex
\mathsf{Ch}(\mathscr{L})
of the undeformed field theory, given in the present case by (
2.14
), because its differential is unaffected by the deformation:
\ell_{1}^{\star}=\ell_{1}
. It follows that the minimal model
{H}^{\bullet}(\mathscr{L}^{\star})
of the braided theory coincides with the minimal model
{H}^{\bullet}(\mathscr{L})
of its commutative counterpart. As a result, the free field theory is unchanged.

On the other hand, the interactions are deformed via the higher brackets
\ell_{n}^{\star}:\text{\Large$\wedge$}^{n}L\longrightarrow L[2-n]
of the braided
L_{\infty}
-algebra
\mathscr{L}^{\star}
for
n\geq 2
. When pulled back to the minimal model by quasi-isomorphisms, the interacting theories differ due to non-trivial braiding in higher brackets.

2.4
Batalin-Vilkovisky Formulation of Braided Scalar Electrodynamics

We study the dynamics of braided scalar electrodynamics in the braided Batalin-Vilkovisky (BV) formalism of
[
2
]
.

Batalin-Vilkovisky Functional.

We extend the Maurer-Cartan functional
S_{\star}
to a functional
S_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}
on
L
, regarded as the space of fields and antifields. With the notation from (
2.6
), we consider a superfield

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}=c+\mathcal{A}+\mathcal{A}^{+}+c^{+}\ ,

(2.40)

viewed as a dynamical field lying in degree 1. We then compute the braided Maurer-Cartan functional (
2.9
) applied to the superfield
{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}
, which defines the BV functional
S_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}({\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}})
.

Using the non-zero brackets and pairings from (
2.27
) and (
2.28
),
the BV functional obtained in this way is given by

\begin{split}S_{{\textrm{\tiny BV}}}(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}})&=S_{\star}(\mathcal{A})+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\langle\mathcal{A}^{+}\,,\,\ell^{\star}_{1}(c)\rangle_{\star}+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\langle c\,,\,\ell^{\star}_{1}(\mathcal{A}^{+})\rangle_{\star}-\tfrac{1}{2}\,\langle c\,,\,\ell_{2}^{\star}(\mathcal{A,A^{+}})+\ell_{2}^{\star}(\mathcal{A^{+},A})\rangle_{\star}\\[4.0pt]
&=S_{\star}(\mathcal{A})+\int_{\mathbbm{R}^{1,3}}\,\mathrm{d}^{4}x\ \bigg(c\star\frac{1}{g}\,\partial_{\mu}A^{+\mu}\\
&\hskip 128.0374pt+\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2}\,c\star\Big(\phi^{+}\star\bar{\phi}-\bar{\phi}^{+}\star\phi\\
&\hskip 184.9429pt+\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(\phi^{+})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(\bar{\phi}\,)-\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(\bar{\phi}^{+})\star\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(\phi)\Big)\bigg)\ .\end{split}

(2.41)

Setting the antifields equal to zero in the BV functional restricts to the Becchi-Rouet-Stora-Tyutin (BRST) fields
(c,\mathcal{A})
and recovers the original braided Maurer-Cartan functional:
S_{{\textrm{\tiny BV}}}(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}})|_{\mathcal{A}^{+}=c^{+}=0}=S_{\star}(\mathcal{A})
. Note that the ghost
c
is absent from the BRST functional, because it completely decouples from the physical fields
\mathcal{A}
due to the abelian nature of the braided
\mathsf{U}(1)
gauge symmetry. In the BV functional (
2.41
), it couples to the scalar antifields through both left and right gauge transformations of the matter fields.

The Space of Fields and Antifields.

It will prove useful to have an explicit description of the fields and antifields of braided scalar electrodynamics in terms of expansions in an appropriate basis. We expand the field/antifield content in a momentum space basis using Fourier transformations.

For the scalar field/antifield pairs
(\phi,\bar{\phi}\,)\in L^{1}
and
(\bar{\phi}^{+},\phi^{+})\in L^{2}
we write

\begin{split}\phi&=\int_{k}\,\widehat{\phi}(k)\ \texttt{e}_{k}\ ,\quad\bar{\phi}=\int_{k}\,\widehat{\bar{\phi}}(k)\ \bar{\mathtt{e}}_{k}\ ,\quad\bar{\phi}^{+}=\int_{k}\,\widehat{\bar{\phi}}{}^{+}(k)\ {\mathtt{e}}^{k}\ ,\quad\phi^{+}=\int_{k}\,\widehat{\phi}{}^{+}(k)\ \bar{\mathtt{e}}^{k}\ .\end{split}

(2.42)

For the scalar basis fields
(\texttt{e}_{k},\bar{\texttt{e}}_{k})\in L^{1}
and
(\bar{\texttt{e}}^{k},\texttt{e}^{k})\in L^{2}
we use the explicit representation as plane waves

\displaystyle\texttt{e}_{k}(x)=\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\,k\cdot x}\quad,\quad\bar{\mathtt{e}}_{k}(x)=\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\,k\cdot x}\quad,\quad\mathtt{e}^{k}(x)=\mathrm{e}^{\,\mathrm{i}\,k\cdot x}\quad,\quad\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{k}=\mathrm{e}^{\,\mathrm{i}\,k\cdot x}\ .

(2.43)

These bases are dual with respect to the cyclic inner product (
2.28
), in the sense that

\displaystyle\langle\texttt{e}_{k},{\mathtt{e}}^{p}\rangle_{\star}=(2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(k-p)=\langle\bar{\texttt{e}}_{k},\bar{\texttt{e}}^{p}\rangle_{\star}\ .

(2.44)

For the gauge field/antifield pair
A\in L^{1}
and
A^{+}\in L^{2}
, we identify the vector space
\Omega^{1}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})
of gauge fields as
(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})^{*}\otimes\Omega^{0}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})
, and dually the vector space of antifields as
\mathbbm{R}^{1,3}\otimes\Omega^{0}(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})
. Given dual bases of covectors
\texttt{v}_{\mu}
and vectors
\texttt{v}^{\mu}
of
(\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})^{*}
and
\mathbbm{R}^{1,3}
respectively, we write

A=\int_{k}\,\widehat{A}_{\mu}(k)\ \mathtt{v}^{\mu}\otimes\texttt{e}_{k}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad A^{+}=\int_{k}\,\widehat{A}{}^{+}{}^{\mu}(k)\ \mathtt{v}_{\mu}\otimes\mathtt{e}^{k}\ .

(2.45)

The dual pairings are given by

\begin{split}\langle\mathtt{v}^{\mu}\otimes\texttt{e}_{k},\mathtt{v}_{\nu}\otimes\mathtt{e}^{p}\rangle_{\star}=(2\pi)^{4}\,\delta_{\nu}^{\mu}\,\delta(k-p)\ .\end{split}

(2.46)

In the following we will omit the tensor product symbols, abbreviating
\mathtt{v}^{\mu}\otimes\texttt{e}_{k}
by
\mathtt{v}^{\mu}\,\texttt{e}_{k}
and
\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\otimes\mathtt{e}^{k}
by
\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{k}
to simplify the notation.

Finally, we expand the ghost field/antifield pair
c\in L^{0}
and
c^{+}\in L^{3}
in a similar vein as

c=\int_{k}\,\widehat{c}(k)\ \widetilde{\mathtt{e}}_{k}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad c^{+}=\int_{k}\,\widehat{c}{}^{+}(k)\ \widetilde{\mathtt{e}}^{k}\ ,

(2.47)

where the scalar basis fields
\widetilde{\texttt{e}}_{k}\in L^{0}
and
\widetilde{\texttt{e}}^{k}\in L^{3}
are given by

\displaystyle\widetilde{\texttt{e}}_{k}(x)=\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\,k\cdot x}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\widetilde{\texttt{e}}^{k}(x)=\mathrm{e}^{\,\mathrm{i}\,k\cdot x}\ .

(2.48)

Their dual pairings are also given by

\displaystyle\langle\widetilde{\texttt{e}}_{k},\widetilde{\texttt{e}}^{p}\rangle_{\star}=(2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(k-p)\ .

(2.49)

The products among momentum space basis fields, twisted by (
2.23
), are given by

\displaystyle\texttt{e}_{k}\star\texttt{e}_{p}=\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2}\,k\cdot\theta\,p}\ \texttt{e}_{k+p}=\mathrm{e}^{\,\mathrm{i}\,p\cdot\theta\,k}\ \texttt{e}_{p}\star\texttt{e}_{k}

(2.50)

where
k\cdot\theta\,p:=k_{\mu}\,\theta^{\mu\nu}\,p_{\nu}=-p\cdot\theta\,k
. The action of the inverse
R
-matrix on tensor products of basis fields is given by

\begin{split}{\mathcal{R}}^{-1}(\texttt{e}_{k}\otimes\texttt{e}_{p})&=\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(\texttt{e}_{k})\otimes\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(\texttt{e}_{p})=\mathrm{e}^{\,\mathrm{i}\,k\cdot\theta\,p}\ \texttt{e}_{k}\otimes\texttt{e}_{p}\ .\end{split}

(2.51)

Similar formulas hold among combinations of the other basis fields from (
2.43
) and (
2.48
).

3
Braided Scalar Quantum Electrodynamics

In this paper we compute correlation functions of polynomial observables for braided scalar quantum electrodynamics using the algebraic framework of braided BV quantization. These observables live in the braided symmetric algebra
\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2]=\bigoplus_{n\geq 0}\,(\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2])^{n}
over
\mathbbm{R}
, defined by twisting the usual symmetric tensor product
\odot
to the braided symmetric tensor product
\odot_{\star}
and graded by polynomial degree. We denote the identity element by
\mathbbm{1}\in(\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2])^{0}
. In this section we lay the foundations for all subsequent calculations and analysis in this paper.

3.1
Extended Batalin-Vilkovisky Formalism

To move from the description in terms of the braided
L_{\infty}
-algebra
\mathscr{L}^{\star}=(L,\ell_{1}^{\star},\ell_{2}^{\star},\ell_{3}^{\star},\langle-,-\rangle_{\star})
to the braided symmetric algebra, we introduce
contracted coordinate functions

[
25
]
in the space
\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}(L[2])\otimes L
.
The cyclic braided
L_{\infty}
-algebra of braided scalar electrodynamics from
section

2.3
is extended to the space of contracted coordinate functions similarly to
[
6
]
, and denoted

\displaystyle\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}(L[2])\otimes\mathscr{L}^{\star}=\big(\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}(L[2])\otimes L\,,\,{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\star}_{1}\,,\,{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\star}_{2}\,,\,{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\star}_{3}\,,\,\langle\!\langle-,-\rangle\!\rangle_{\star}\big)\ .

(3.1)

In this extended framework, the BV functional
S_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}({\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}})\in\mathbbm{R}
from (
2.41
) is lifted to a translation invariant functional
{\mathcal{S}}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}({\boldsymbol{\xi}})\in(\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2])^{0}
, called the extended BV functional. It is defined by the Maurer-Cartan functional
\mathcal{S}(\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}(L[2])\otimes\mathscr{L}^{\star})
applied to the translation invariant contracted coordinate function
\boldsymbol{\xi}\in(\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}(L[2])\otimes L)^{1}
of symmetric tensor and total degree 1. In terms of the decompositions of
section

2.4
, this is given by

\displaystyle\begin{split}\boldsymbol{\xi}&=\int_{k}\,\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{k}\otimes\mathtt{v}^{\mu}\,\texttt{e}_{k}+\mathtt{e}^{k}\otimes\texttt{e}_{k}+\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{k}\otimes\bar{\mathtt{e}}_{k}\\
&\qquad\,+\int_{k}\,\widetilde{\mathtt{e}}^{k}\otimes\widetilde{\mathtt{e}}_{k}+\widetilde{\mathtt{e}}_{k}\otimes\widetilde{\mathtt{e}}^{k}+\mathtt{v}^{\mu}\,\texttt{e}_{k}\otimes\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{k}+\texttt{e}_{k}\otimes\mathtt{e}^{k}+\bar{\mathtt{e}}_{k}\otimes\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{k}\ .\end{split}

(3.2)

The first line of (
3.2
) represents the
physical
part of the extended superfield for the extended theory, corresponding to pairs
\mathcal{A}^{+}\otimes\mathcal{A}
of antifields and fields in
L[2]^{0}\otimes L^{1}
, which is the part relevant to the computation of correlation functions of physical fields
\mathcal{A}
. The second line incorporates braided gauge symmetries: the first term corresponds to the ghost antifield/field pairs
c^{+}\otimes c
and
c\otimes c^{+}
, living in
L[2]^{1}\otimes L^{0}
and
L[2]^{-2}\otimes L^{3}
respectively, while the remaining terms correspond to
\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{A}^{+}
in
L[2]^{-1}\otimes L^{2}
.

The extended BV functional is a 0-cochain given in terms of the extended cyclic inner product and extended brackets by

\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}=\tfrac{1}{2!}\,\langle\!\langle\boldsymbol{\xi},\boldsymbol{\ell}_{1}^{\star}(\boldsymbol{\xi})\rangle\!\rangle_{\star}-\tfrac{1}{3!}\,\langle\!\langle\boldsymbol{\xi},\boldsymbol{\ell}^{\star}_{2}(\boldsymbol{\xi},\boldsymbol{\xi})\rangle\!\rangle_{\star}-\tfrac{1}{4!}\,\langle\!\langle\boldsymbol{\xi},\boldsymbol{\ell}^{\star}_{3}(\boldsymbol{\xi},\boldsymbol{\xi},\boldsymbol{\xi})\rangle\!\rangle_{\star}\ .

(3.3)

The first term contains the free part
\mathcal{S}_{0}
. The remaining terms define the interaction part of the extended BV functional which we write as a sum
\mathcal{S}_{\rm int}+\mathcal{S}_{{\textrm{\tiny BRST}}}
, where

\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{\rm int}=\mathcal{S}_{\rm int}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}+\mathcal{S}_{\rm int}^{\textrm{\tiny(4)}}

(3.4)

represents respectively the trivalent and quadrivalent interactions among the physical fields
\mathcal{A}
, while

\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{{\textrm{\tiny BRST}}}=\mathcal{S}_{{\textrm{\tiny BRST}}}^{\textrm{\tiny(2)}}+\mathcal{S}_{{\textrm{\tiny BRST}}}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}

(3.5)

represents respectively the bivalent and trivalent interactions of the ghost
c
with the physical fields
\mathcal{A}
and their antifields
\mathcal{A}^{+}
. We proceed to analyse these four interaction terms in turn.

{\boldsymbol{\phi\bar{\phi}A}}
Vertex.

Using strict cyclicity of the inner product to reduce the number of terms to two, together with translation invariance of the contracted coordinate functions, we compute the trivalent interaction from the physical part of the extended superfield (
3.2
) as

\begin{split}\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int}&=-\tfrac{1}{3!}\,\langle\!\langle\boldsymbol{\xi},\boldsymbol{\ell}^{\star}_{2}(\boldsymbol{\xi},\boldsymbol{\xi})\rangle\!\rangle_{\star}\\[4.0pt]
&=-\int_{k_{1},k_{2},k_{3}}\,\langle\!\langle\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{k_{1}}\otimes\mathtt{v}^{\mu}\,\texttt{e}_{k_{1}}\,,\,\boldsymbol{\ell}_{2}^{\star}(\mathtt{e}^{k_{2}}\otimes\texttt{e}_{k_{2}},\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{k_{3}}\otimes\bar{\mathtt{e}}_{k_{3}})\rangle\!\rangle_{\star}\\[4.0pt]
&=-\int_{k_{1},k_{2},k_{3}}\,\langle\!\langle\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{k_{1}}\otimes\mathtt{v}^{\mu}\,\texttt{e}_{k_{1}}\,,\,(\mathtt{e}^{k_{2}}\odot_{\star}\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{k_{3}}))\otimes\ell_{2}^{\star}(\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(\texttt{e}_{k_{2}}),\bar{\mathtt{e}}_{k_{3}})\rangle\!\rangle_{\star}\\[4.0pt]
&=-\int_{k_{1},k_{2},k_{3}}\,\mathrm{e}^{\,\mathrm{i}\,k_{2}\cdot\theta\,k_{3}}\ \mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{k_{1}}\odot_{\star}\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(\mathtt{e}^{k_{2}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{k_{3}})\ \langle\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(\mathtt{v}^{\mu}\,\texttt{e}_{k_{1}})\,,\,\ell_{2}^{\star}(\texttt{e}_{k_{2}},\bar{\mathtt{e}}_{k_{3}})\rangle_{\star}\\[4.0pt]
&=-\int_{k_{1},k_{2},k_{3}}\,\mathrm{e}^{\,\mathrm{i}\,\sum\limits_{i<j}\,k_{i}\cdot\theta\,k_{j}}\ \mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{k_{1}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{e}^{k_{2}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{k_{3}}\ \langle\mathtt{v}^{\mu}\,\texttt{e}_{k_{1}}\,,\,\ell_{2}^{\star}(\texttt{e}_{k_{2}},\bar{\mathtt{e}}_{k_{3}})\rangle_{\star}\ .\end{split}

(3.6)

Using the last entry of (
2.27
) to compute

\begin{split}\langle\mathtt{v}^{\mu}\,\texttt{e}_{k_{1}}\,,\,\ell_{2}^{\star}(\texttt{e}_{k_{2}},\bar{\mathtt{e}}_{k_{3}})\rangle_{\star}&=\mathrm{i}\,g\,\langle\mathtt{v}^{\mu}\,\texttt{e}_{k_{1}},\texttt{e}_{k_{2}}\star\texttt{v}_{\nu}\,\partial^{\nu}\bar{\mathtt{e}}_{k_{3}}-\texttt{v}_{\nu}\,\partial^{\nu}\texttt{e}_{k_{2}}\star\bar{\mathtt{e}}_{k_{3}}\rangle_{\star}\\[4.0pt]
&=g\,(k_{3}-k_{2})^{\mu}\ \mathrm{e}^{-\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2}\,\sum\limits_{i<j}\,k_{i}\cdot\theta\,k_{j}}\ (2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(k_{1}+k_{2}+k_{3})\ ,\end{split}

(3.7)

this evaluates to

\begin{split}\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int}=\int_{k_{1},k_{2},k_{3}}\,V^{\mu}_{3}(k_{1},k_{2},k_{3})\ \mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{k_{1}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{e}^{k_{2}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{k_{3}}\ ,\end{split}

(3.8)

where the scalar-scalar-photon vertex is given by

\begin{split}V^{\mu}_{3}(k_{1},k_{2},k_{3})=g\ \mathrm{e}^{\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2}\,\sum\limits_{i<j}\,k_{i}\cdot\theta\,k_{j}}\,(k_{2}-k_{3})^{\mu}\ (2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(k_{1}+k_{2}+k_{3})\ .\end{split}

(3.9)

(3.10)

where the photon field
A
is represented by a wavy line and the scalar fields
(\phi,\bar{\phi}\,)
by directed straight lines.

{\boldsymbol{\phi\bar{\phi}AA}}
Vertex.

The four-point interaction is given by

\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(4)}}_{\rm int}=-\tfrac{1}{4!}\,\langle\!\langle\boldsymbol{\xi},\boldsymbol{\ell}_{3}^{\star}(\boldsymbol{\xi},\boldsymbol{\xi},\boldsymbol{\xi})\rangle\!\rangle_{\star}\ .

(3.11)

Since the extended bracket and cyclic structure are compatible, we consider the cyclically inequivalent terms, of which there are three.
We then use the translation invariance of contracted coordinate functions
\boldsymbol{\xi}
, and strict cyclicity of the inner product to identify all such terms.
This gives

\begin{split}\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(4)}}_{\rm int}&=-\frac{1}{2}\,\int_{k_{1},k_{2},k_{3},k_{4}}\,\langle\!\langle\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{k_{1}}\otimes\mathtt{v}^{\mu}\,\texttt{e}_{k_{1}}\,,\,\boldsymbol{\ell}_{3}^{\star}(\mathtt{e}^{k_{2}}\otimes\texttt{e}_{k_{2}},\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{k_{3}}\otimes\bar{\mathtt{e}}_{k_{3}},\mathtt{v}_{\nu}{\mathtt{e}}^{k_{4}}\otimes\mathtt{v}^{\nu}{\mathtt{e}}_{k_{4}})\rangle\!\rangle_{\star}\\[4.0pt]
&=-\frac{1}{2}\,\int_{k_{1},k_{2},k_{3},k_{4}}\,\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{k_{1}}\odot_{\star}\mathsf{R}_{\delta}\big(\mathtt{e}^{k_{2}}\odot_{\star}\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(\bar{\texttt{e}}^{k_{3}})\odot_{\star}\mathsf{R}_{\beta}\,\mathsf{R}_{\gamma}(\mathtt{v}_{\nu}\,\texttt{e}^{k_{4}})\big)\\
&\hskip 113.81102pt\times\langle\mathsf{R}^{\delta}(\mathtt{v}^{\mu}\,\texttt{e}_{k_{1}})\,,\,\ell_{3}^{\star}(\mathsf{R}^{\beta}\,\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(\texttt{e}_{k_{2}}),\mathsf{R}^{\gamma}(\bar{\texttt{e}}_{k_{3}}),\mathtt{v}^{\nu}\,\texttt{e}_{k_{4}})\rangle_{\star}\\[4.0pt]
&=-\frac{1}{2}\,\int_{k_{1},k_{2},k_{3},k_{4}}\,\mathrm{e}^{\,\mathrm{i}\,\sum\limits_{i<j}\,k_{i}\cdot\theta\,k_{j}}\ \mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{k_{1}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{e}^{k_{2}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\texttt{e}}^{k_{3}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{v}_{\nu}\,\texttt{e}^{k_{4}}\\
&\hskip 170.71652pt\times\langle\mathtt{v}^{\mu}\,\texttt{e}_{k_{1}}\,,\,\ell_{3}^{\star}(\texttt{e}_{k_{2}},\bar{\texttt{e}}_{k_{3}},\mathtt{v}^{\nu}\,\texttt{e}_{k_{4}})\rangle_{\star}\ .\end{split}

(3.12)

Using the last entry of (
2.27
) we compute

\begin{split}\langle\mathtt{v}^{\mu}\,\texttt{e}_{k_{1}}\,,\,\ell_{3}^{\star}(\texttt{e}_{k_{2}},\bar{\texttt{e}}_{k_{3}},\mathtt{v}^{\nu}\,\texttt{e}_{k_{4}})\rangle_{\star}&=-2\,g^{2}\,\langle\texttt{v}^{\mu}\,\texttt{e}_{k_{1}},\texttt{e}_{k_{2}}\star\bar{\texttt{e}}_{k_{3}}\star\texttt{v}^{\nu}\,\texttt{e}_{k_{4}}\rangle_{\star}\\[4.0pt]
&=-2\,g^{2}\,\eta^{\mu\nu}\,\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2}\,\sum\limits_{i<j}\,k_{i}\cdot\theta\,k_{j}}\ (2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(k_{1}+k_{2}+k_{3}+k_{4})\ .\end{split}

(3.13)

This gives the braided symmetric four-point interaction

\begin{split}\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(4)}}_{\rm int}=\int_{k_{1},k_{2},k_{3},k_{4}}\,V_{4}^{\mu\nu}(k_{1},k_{2},k_{3},k_{4})\ \mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{k_{1}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{e}^{k_{2}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{k_{3}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{v}_{\nu}\,\mathtt{e}^{k_{4}}\ ,\end{split}

(3.14)

where the four-vertex function is given by

\begin{split}V_{4}^{\mu\nu}(k_{1},k_{2},k_{3},k_{4})=g^{2}\,\eta^{\mu\nu}\,\mathrm{e}^{\,\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2}\,\sum\limits_{i<j}\,k_{i}\cdot\theta\,k_{j}}\ (2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(k_{1}+k_{2}+k_{3}+k_{4})\ .\end{split}

(3.15)

This is represented graphically by

(3.16)

{\boldsymbol{cA^{+}}}
Vertex.

Using (
2.27
) together with cyclicity of the inner product, we find that the lift of the term
\langle\mathcal{A}^{+},\ell^{\star}_{1}(c)\rangle_{\star}
in the full BV functional (
2.41
) is given by

\begin{split}\mathcal{S}_{{\textrm{\tiny BRST}}}^{\textrm{\tiny(2)}}&=\int_{k_{1},k_{2}}\,\langle\!\langle\mathtt{v}^{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}_{k_{1}}\otimes\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{k_{1}}\,,\,\boldsymbol{\ell}_{1}^{\star}(\mathtt{\widetilde{e}}^{k_{2}}\otimes\mathtt{\widetilde{e}}_{k_{2}})\rangle\!\rangle_{\star}=\int_{k_{1},k_{2}}\,V_{2\,\mu}^{\textrm{\tiny BRST}}(k_{1},k_{2})\ \mathtt{v}^{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}_{k_{1}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{\widetilde{e}}^{k_{2}}\ ,\end{split}

(3.17)

where the linear interaction vertex is given by

\displaystyle V_{2\,\mu}^{\textrm{\tiny BRST}}(k_{1},k_{2})=\tfrac{\mathrm{i}}{g}\,k_{1\,\mu}\ (2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(k_{1}-k_{2})\ .

(3.18)

This corresponds to braided gauge transformations of the photon field.
Note the sign appearing from
\boldsymbol{\ell}_{1}^{\star}(\mathtt{\widetilde{e}}^{k_{2}}\otimes\mathtt{\widetilde{e}}_{k_{2}})=-\mathtt{\widetilde{e}}^{k_{2}}\otimes\ell_{1}^{\star}(\mathtt{\widetilde{e}}_{k_{2}})
due to the grading of the ghosts, see
[
25
]
.

We represent this graphically by the diagram

\mu
k_{1}
k_{2}

(3.19)

where the photon antifield
A^{+}
is depicted with the dotted pattern and the ghost field
c
with the dashed pattern.

{\boldsymbol{c\bar{\phi}\phi^{+}{+}c\phi\bar{\phi}^{+}}}
Vertex.

The three-point BRST vertex corresponding to braided gauge transformations of the scalar fields is calculated from the lift of the terms
-\frac{1}{2}\,\langle c\,,\,\ell_{2}^{\star}(\mathcal{A,A^{+}})+\ell_{2}^{\star}(\mathcal{A}^{+},\mathcal{A})\rangle_{\star}
in the full BV functional (
2.41
).
Using the brackets (
2.27p
) and performing completely analogous calculations to those above, we find that this contributes

\begin{split}\mathcal{S}_{\textrm{\tiny BRST}}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}&=-\int_{k_{1},k_{2},k_{3}}\,\langle\!\langle\mathtt{\widetilde{e}}^{k_{3}}\otimes\mathtt{\widetilde{e}}_{k_{3}}\,,\,\boldsymbol{\ell}_{2}^{\star}(\mathtt{e}^{k_{1}}\otimes\mathtt{e}_{k_{1}}+\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{k_{1}}\otimes\bar{\mathtt{e}}_{k_{1}}\ ,\ {\mathtt{e}}_{k_{2}}\otimes{\mathtt{e}}^{k_{2}}+\bar{\mathtt{e}}_{k_{2}}\otimes\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{k_{2}})\rangle\!\rangle_{\star}\\[4.0pt]
&=\int_{k_{1},k_{2},k_{3}}\,V_{3}^{{\textrm{\tiny BRST}}}(k_{1},k_{2},k_{3})\ \big(-\widetilde{\mathtt{e}}^{k_{3}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{e}_{k_{2}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{e}^{k_{1}}\ +\ \mathtt{\widetilde{e}}^{k_{3}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}_{k_{2}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{k_{1}}\big)\end{split}

(3.20)

to the extended BV functional, where

\displaystyle V_{3}^{\textrm{\tiny BRST}}(k_{1},k_{2},k_{3})=\mathrm{i}\ \mathrm{e}^{\,\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2}\,\sum\limits_{i<j}\,k_{i}\cdot\theta\,k_{j}}\ (2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(k_{1}-k_{2}+k_{3})\ .

(3.21)

This is represented by the diagrams

3.2
Homological Perturbation Theory

To study correlation functions of braided scalar quantum electrodynamics, we need to extend the deformation retract of the original theory from
section

2.2
to the braided symmetric algebra
\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2]
.
We use the “symmetric tensor trick” (reviewed in
[
32
]
) to extend the retract to a contraction of symmetric algebras, generalized to the symmetric monoidal category with non-trivial braiding isomorphism in which our
L_{\infty}
-algebra
\mathscr{L}^{\star}
lives.

(3.23)

Here we used translation invariance of the differential
\ell_{1}^{\star}
of the braided
L_{\infty}
-algebra
\mathscr{L}^{\star}
to extend it to a differential
\boldsymbol{\ell}_{1}^{\star}:\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2]\longrightarrow(\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2])[1]
of symmetric degree
0
as a strict graded derivation.
The maps in (
3.23
) are all of symmetric degree
0
while their respective total degrees are inherited from the minimal model of
section

2.2
.

The homotopy equivalence is captured by the relation

\boldsymbol{\ell}^{\star}_{1}\circ\mathsf{H}+\mathsf{H}\circ\boldsymbol{\ell}^{\star}_{1}+\mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2]}=\mathsf{I}_{0}\circ\mathsf{P}_{0}\ .

(3.24)

By the isomorphism
L[2]\simeq L[1]^{*}
induced by the cyclic inner product, the degree 0 cochain maps
\iota
and
p
extend as algebra homomorphisms with
\mathsf{I}_{0}={}^{\rm t}p
and
\mathsf{P}_{0}={}^{\rm t}\iota
in symmetric degree
1
. Since any deformation retract can be refined to a strong deformation retract, we can assume without loss of generality the relations

\begin{split}\mathsf{P}_{0}\circ\mathsf{I}_{0}=\mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}H^{\bullet}(L[2])}\quad,\quad\mathsf{P}_{0}\circ\mathsf{H}=0\quad,\quad\mathsf{H}\circ\mathsf{I}_{0}=0\quad,\quad\mathsf{H}^{2}=0\end{split}\ .

(3.25)

Vacuum correlation functions are computed by projecting to the trivial degree
0
subspace
\mathbbm{R}\subset\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}H^{\bullet}(L[2])

[
33
,
34
]
; this is done using the map
\mathsf{P}_{0}:\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2]\longrightarrow(\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}H^{\bullet}(L[2]))^{0}
defined by

\displaystyle\mathsf{P}_{0}(\mathbbm{1})=1\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\mathsf{P}_{0}(\varphi_{1}\odot_{\star}\cdots\odot_{\star}\varphi_{n})=0\ ,

(3.26)

for all
\varphi_{i}\in L[2]
, with
i=1,\dots,n
. Then
\mathsf{I}_{0}:\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}H^{\bullet}(L[2])\longrightarrow(\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2])^{0}
is the canonical inclusion
\mathbbm{R}\subset\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2]
sending all higher degree elements to zero. The associated contracting homotopy is given by the map
\mathsf{H}:\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}(L[2])\longrightarrow\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}(L[2])[-1]
of symmetric degree 0 defined as

\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathsf{H}(\mathbbm{1})&=0\ ,\\[4.0pt]
\mathsf{H}(\varphi_{1}\odot_{\star}\cdots\odot_{\star}\varphi_{n})&=\frac{1}{n}\,\sum_{i=1}^{n}\,\pm\ \varphi_{1}\odot_{\star}\cdots\odot_{\star}\varphi_{i-1}\odot_{\star}{\sf h}(\varphi_{i})\odot_{\star}\varphi_{i+1}\odot_{\star}\cdots\odot_{\star}\varphi_{n}\ ,\end{split}

(3.27)

where we used translation invariance of
{\sf h}
in (
3.27
) which trivializes the actions of
R
-matrices; here and in the following all explicit Koszul sign factors
\pm
can be found in
[
5
]
.

The braided extension of the homological perturbation lemma
[
5
]
allows one to deform this homotopy equivalence data with differential
\boldsymbol{\ell}^{\star}_{1}+\boldsymbol{\delta}
for “small” translation invariant perturbation map
\boldsymbol{\delta}
, i.e. for which the map
\mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2]}-\boldsymbol{\delta}\,\mathsf{H}
is invertible, while preserving the strong deformation retract structure (
3.25
).
The deformation retract (
3.23
) is then perturbed to

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2],\boldsymbol{\ell}^{\star}_{1}+\boldsymbol{\delta})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}H^{\bullet}(L[2]),{\boldsymbol{\delta}}^{\prime})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{H}+\mathsf{H_{{\boldsymbol{\delta}}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{P}_{0}+\mathsf{P}_{\boldsymbol{\delta}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{I}_{0}+\mathsf{I_{{\boldsymbol{\delta}}}}}

(3.28)

where the projection operator is modified by the map
\mathsf{P}_{\boldsymbol{\delta}}:\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2]\longrightarrow\mathbbm{R}=(\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}H^{\bullet}(L[2]))^{0}
given by

\begin{split}\mathsf{P}_{{\boldsymbol{\delta}}}&=\mathsf{P}_{0}\,\big(\mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2]}-\boldsymbol{\delta}\,\mathsf{H}\big)^{-1}\,\boldsymbol{\delta}\,\mathsf{H}=\mathsf{P}_{0}\,\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\,(\boldsymbol{\delta}\,\mathsf{H})^{k}\ .\end{split}

(3.29)

The explicit forms of the remaining perturbed maps in (
3.28
) can be found in
[
5
]
.

For a perturbation datum
{\boldsymbol{\delta}}
, we denote the perturbed differential by

\displaystyle Q_{{\boldsymbol{\delta}}}:=\boldsymbol{\ell}^{\star}_{1}+{{\boldsymbol{\delta}}}\ .

(3.30)

Free Theory.

The free theory is constructed from the perturbed differential

\displaystyle Q_{\hbar}:=\boldsymbol{\ell}_{1}^{\star}+\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,{\mathsf{\Delta}}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\ ,

(3.31)

which is an example of a quantum differential, see e.g.
[
35
]
.
The equivariant cochain map

\displaystyle\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}:\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2]\longrightarrow(\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2])[1]

(3.32)

of symmetric degree
-2
is called the BV Laplacian, since it reduces the symmetric degree by
2
. It satisfies
({\mathsf{\Delta}}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}})^{2}=0
and
\boldsymbol{\ell}_{1}^{\star}\circ{\mathsf{\Delta}}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}=-{\mathsf{\Delta}}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\circ\boldsymbol{\ell}_{1}^{\star}
, which together guarantee
(Q_{\hbar})^{2}=0
. Explicitly, it is defined by extending the differential

\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}(\mathbbm{1})=0&\qquad,\qquad\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}(\varphi_{1})=0\qquad,\qquad\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}(\varphi_{1}\odot_{\star}\varphi_{2})=\langle\varphi_{1},\varphi_{2}\rangle_{\star}\,\mathbbm{1}\end{split}

(3.33)

on the symmetric algebra to

\begin{split}\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}(\varphi_{1}\odot_{\star}\cdots\odot_{\star}\varphi_{n})&=\sum_{i<j}\,\pm\,\langle\varphi_{i},\mathsf{R}_{\alpha_{i+1}}\cdots\mathsf{R}_{\alpha_{j-1}}(\varphi_{j})\rangle_{\star}\ \varphi_{1}\odot_{\star}\cdots\odot_{\star}\varphi_{i-1}\\
&\hskip 34.14322pt\odot_{\star}\mathsf{R}^{\alpha_{i+1}}(\varphi_{i+1})\odot_{\star}\cdots\odot_{\star}\mathsf{R}^{\alpha_{j-1}}(\varphi_{j-1})\odot_{\star}\varphi_{j+1}\odot_{\star}\cdots\odot_{\star}\varphi_{n}\ ,\end{split}

(3.34)

for all
\varphi_{1},\dots,\varphi_{n}\in L[2]
.

This yields the strong deformation retract

(3.35)

Since
\mathsf{H}\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{I}_{0}=0
,
the induced BV differential on
\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}H^{\bullet}(L[2])
is given by
[
36
]

\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}^{\prime}=\mathsf{P}_{0}\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{I}_{0}
.

Interacting Theory.

The interacting quantum theory is constructed by further deforming the BV Laplacian with the interactions
\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{int}}
from
section

3.1
, giving the degree 1 small perturbation

\boldsymbol{\delta}_{\hbar,{\rm int}}=\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,{\mathsf{\Delta}}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}+\left\{\mathcal{S}_{\rm int},-\right\}_{\star}\ ,

(3.36)

and the quantum differential
Q_{\hbar,{\rm int}}:=\boldsymbol{\ell}_{1}^{\star}+\boldsymbol{\delta}_{\hbar,{\rm int}}
.
The BV antibracket

\displaystyle\{-,-\}_{\star}:\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2]\otimes\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2]\longrightarrow(\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2])[1]

(3.37)

is the braided
(-1)
-shifted Poisson structure
defined on generators
\varphi_{1},\varphi_{2}\in L[2]
using the cyclic inner product
\langle-,-\rangle_{\star}
of the braided
L_{\infty}
-algebra
\mathscr{L}^{\star}
as

\displaystyle\{\varphi_{1},\varphi_{2}\}_{\star}=\langle\varphi_{1},\varphi_{2}\rangle_{\star}\,\mathbbm{1}=\pm\,\,\{\mathsf{R}_{\alpha}(\varphi_{2}),\mathsf{R}^{\alpha}(\varphi_{1})\}_{\star}\ ,

(3.38)

and extended as a braided graded derivation in each of its slots.

Because of cyclicity of the inner product
\langle-,-\rangle_{\star}
, the differential
{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\star}_{1}
is compatible with the antibracket, making
\big(\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2],{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\star}_{1},\{-,-\}_{\star})
into a braided
P_{0}
-algebra
[
5
]
. The braided
L_{\infty}
-structure implies that the full classical theory with BV functional
\mathcal{S}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}
from (
3.3
) satisfies the classical master equation
\{\mathcal{S}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}},\mathcal{S}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\}_{\star}=0
.
On the other hand, the failure of the BV Laplacian to be a strict graded derivation of the braided commutative product is measured by

\displaystyle\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}(a_{1}\odot_{\star}a_{2})=\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}(a_{1})\odot_{\star}a_{2}\pm a_{1}\odot_{\star}\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}(a_{2})+\{a_{1},a_{2}\}_{\star}\ ,

(3.39)

for all
a_{1},a_{2}\in\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2]
, making
\big(\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2],{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\star}_{1},\left\{-,-\right\}_{\star},\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\big)
into a differential graded braided BV algebra. This implies that the BV differential act as a strict graded derivation of the Poisson structure
[
5
]
:

\begin{split}\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}(\left\{a_{1},a_{2}\right\}_{\star})=\{\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}(a_{1}),a_{2}\}_{\star}\pm\{a_{1},\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}(a_{2})\}_{\star}\ .\end{split}

(3.40)

(3.41)

The nilpotency condition for the deformed differential
{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\star}_{1}+\boldsymbol{\delta}_{\hbar,{\rm int}}
on
\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2]
is equivalent to the quantum master equation

\boldsymbol{\ell}_{1}^{\star}(\mathcal{S}_{\rm int})+\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,{\mathsf{\Delta}}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}(\mathcal{S}_{\rm int})+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\{\mathcal{S}_{\rm int},\mathcal{S}_{\rm int}\}_{\star}=0

(3.42)

for the degree 0 cochain
\mathcal{S}_{\rm int}
, which follows trivially from the classical master equation for
\mathcal{S}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}
together with
{\mathsf{\Delta}}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}(\mathcal{S}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}})=0

[
5
,
2
,
6
]
.

Using the Homological Perturbation Lemma.

In this paper we will compute various one-loop correlation functions of physical fields in braided scalar quantum electrodynamics. Correlation functions are computed via the homological perturbation lemma by applying the perturbed projector (
3.29
) with the deformation retract (
3.41
) to insertions of
antifields
on external states at positions
x_{i}\in\mathbbm{R}^{1,3}
.

For this, we use the momentum space decompositions (
2.45
) and (
2.42
) for the field and antifield content of braided scalar electrodynamics.
The external antifield states are related to a position space basis by Fourier transformation

\delta^{A_{\mu}}_{x_{i}}=\int_{p_{i}}\,\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{p_{i}}\ \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\,p_{i}\cdot x_{i}}\quad,\quad\delta^{\bar{\phi}}_{x_{i}}=\int_{p_{i}}\,\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{p_{i}}\ \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\,p_{i}\cdot x_{i}}\quad,\quad\delta^{\phi}_{x_{i}}=\int_{p_{i}}\,\mathtt{e}^{p_{i}}\ \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\,p_{i}\cdot x_{i}}\ .

(3.43)

Contractions of states are achieved through application of the operator
{\mathsf{\Delta}}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H}
.
By contracting external states with each other using the cyclic structure and contracting homotopy, we recover the respective free propagators in position space: for the scalar fields

\langle\delta_{x_{i}}^{\phi},\mathsf{h}\,\delta_{x_{j}}^{\bar{\phi}}\rangle_{\star}=-\mathsf{G}(x_{i}-x_{j})=-\int_{k}\,\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(k)\ \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\,k\cdot(x_{i}-x_{j})}\ ,

(3.44)

and similarly for the photon contractions.
For the scalar fields, contractions between internal and external states yield

\langle\mathtt{e}^{k_{i}}\,,\,\mathsf{h}\,\delta_{x_{j}}^{\bar{\phi}}\rangle_{\star}=-\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(k_{i})\,\mathrm{e}^{\,\mathrm{i}\,k_{i}\cdot x_{j}}=\langle\mathsf{h}\,\mathtt{e}^{k_{i}}\,,\,\delta_{x_{j}}^{\bar{\phi}}\rangle_{\star}\ ,

(3.45)

and similarly for the photon internal/external state contractions.

In this paper we mostly use the momentum space representation, electing to Fourier transform the correlation function at the source.
Internal contractions of two fields using
\Delta_{{\textrm{\tiny BV}}}\,\mathsf{H}
in momentum space are described by (
2.45
), (
2.42
) and (
2.43
) together with (
2.22
). They satisfy

\langle\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{k_{i}},\mathsf{h}\,\mathtt{v}_{\nu}\,\mathtt{e}^{k_{j}}\rangle_{\star}=-\mathsf{\tilde{D}}(k_{i})\,\mathsf{\tilde{\Pi}}_{\mu\nu}(k_{i})\ (2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(k_{i}+k_{j})

(3.46)

for the photon field, which we represent graphically by the wavy line

(3.47)

and

\langle\mathtt{e}^{k_{i}},\mathsf{h}\,\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{k_{j}}\rangle_{\star}=-\mathsf{\tilde{G}}(k_{i})\ (2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(k_{i}+k_{j})

(3.48)

for the scalar fields, which we represent graphically by the directed straight line
