(3.49)

Finally, the interaction vertices are generated by the BV antibrackets with the translation invariant degree
0
extended action functionals (
3.8
) and (
3.14
) from
section

3.1
:

\begin{split}\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int},-\}_{\star}&=\int_{k_{1},k_{2},k_{3}}\,V^{\mu}_{3}(k_{1},k_{2},k_{3})\ \big\{\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{k_{1}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{e}^{k_{2}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{k_{3}},-\big\}_{\star}\ ,\\[4.0pt]
\{\mathcal{S}_{\rm int}^{{\textrm{\tiny(4)}}},-\}_{\star}&=\int_{k_{1},k_{2},k_{3},k_{4}}\,V_{4}^{\mu\nu}(k_{1},k_{2},k_{3},k_{4})\ \big\{\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{k_{1}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{e}^{k_{2}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{k_{3}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{v}_{\nu}\,\mathtt{e}^{k_{4}},-\big\}_{\star}\ .\end{split}

(3.50)

Thanks to momentum conservation across vertices, the expansions (
3.50
) in terms of a basis of antifields can always be cyclically rotated to better suit calculations; we will always act from the left. For the same reason, the interacting action functional acts as a
strict
graded derivation on
\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2]
, that is, the
R
-matrices trivialise when moving the vertex across a braided symmetric product; equivalently,
\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{int}}
is translation invariant. We will only consider degree 0 elements of
L[2]
, so this further restricts to a derivation:

\begin{split}\left\{\mathcal{S}_{\rm int},\varphi_{1}\odot_{\star}\varphi_{2}\right\}_{\star}=\left\{\mathcal{S}_{\rm int},\varphi_{1}\right\}_{\star}\odot_{\star}\varphi_{2}+\varphi_{1}\odot_{\star}\left\{\mathcal{S}_{\rm int},\varphi_{2}\right\}_{\star}\end{split}\ ,

(3.51)

for
\varphi_{1},\varphi_{2}\in L[2]^{0}
.

4
Correlation Functions at One-Loop

In this paper we are interested in the
n
-point correlation functions of braided scalar quantum electrodynamics by perturbed projection maps (
3.29
) acting on antifield insertions of Dirac distributions supported at spacetime points
x_{i}
.
Our basis of test Dirac distributions is given by the set
\big\{\delta_{x_{i}}^{\phi},\delta_{x_{i}}^{\bar{\phi}},\delta_{x_{i}}^{A_{\mu}}\big\}\subset L[2]^{0}
described in
section

3.2
, of which a generic element is denoted
\delta^{\mathcal{A}_{i}}_{x_{i}}
.

We define correlation functions in this setting as

\begin{split}\mathsf{G}^{{\boldsymbol{\delta}}}_{\mathcal{A}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{A}_{n}}({x_{1}},\ldots,{x_{n}})&=\mathsf{P}_{{\boldsymbol{\delta}}}\big(\delta^{\mathcal{A}_{1}}_{x_{1}}\odot_{\star}\cdots\odot_{\star}\delta^{\mathcal{A}_{n}}_{x_{n}}\big)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\,\mathsf{P}_{0}\,({{\boldsymbol{\delta}}}\,\mathsf{H})^{k}\,\big(\delta^{\mathcal{A}_{1}}_{x_{1}}\odot_{\star}\cdots\odot_{\star}\delta^{\mathcal{A}_{n}}_{x_{n}}\big)\ .\end{split}

(4.1)

Because only
\mathsf{P}_{0}(\mathbbm{1})=1
is non-zero, the correlation function is a map

\displaystyle\mathsf{G}_{n}^{{\boldsymbol{\delta}}}:(\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2])^{0}\longrightarrow\Omega^{0}\big((\mathbbm{R}^{1,3})^{\times n}\big)\ ,

(4.2)

understood in a distributional sense. For the same reason only correlators involving the same number of scalar antifields
\delta_{x_{i}}^{\phi}
and their conjugates
\delta_{x_{i}}^{\bar{\phi}}
are non-vanishing, as only such pairs can lead to non-vanishing inner products; this is the statement of charge conjugation symmetry in braided scalar QED. We will generically work with the strong deformation retract (
3.41
) for which

\mathsf{G}_{n}^{\hbar,{\rm int}}:=\mathsf{G}_{n}^{{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{\hbar,{\rm int}}}
is a formal power series in
\hbar
and
g
; we write
\mathsf{G}_{n}^{\hbar}
for the correlators of the free field theory associated to the deformation retract (
3.35
).

Alternatively, we can decompose a general antifield in terms of a basis
\mathtt{e}^{p_{i}}_{\mathcal{A}_{i}}
of plane waves dual to a basis
\mathtt{e}_{p_{i}}^{\mathcal{A}_{i}}\in L[2]^{0}
as

\begin{split}\delta^{\mathcal{A}_{i}}_{x_{i}}=\int_{p_{i}}\,\mathtt{e}_{\mathcal{A}_{i}}^{p_{i}}\ \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\,p_{i}\cdot x_{i}}\ .\end{split}

(4.3)

This defines the
n
-point correlation function in momentum space as

\begin{split}\mathsf{\tilde{G}}^{{\boldsymbol{\delta}}}_{\mathcal{A}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{A}_{n}}(p_{1},\ldots,p_{n})&=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\,\mathsf{P}_{0}\,(\boldsymbol{\delta}\,\mathsf{H})^{k}\,\big(\mathtt{e}^{p_{1}}_{\mathcal{A}_{1}}\odot_{\star}\cdots\odot_{\star}\mathtt{e}^{p_{n}}_{\mathcal{A}_{n}}\big)\ .\end{split}

(4.4)

This prescription computes both connected and disconnected diagrams with
n
external propagators. In this section we detail the calculation of several correlators up to one-loop order.

These are vacuum correlation functions in the terminology of
[
6
]
. This is unlike the computation of scattering amplitudes done in
[
31
,
37
]
, where the cyclic
L_{\infty}
-structure is pulled back to the minimal model, which yields infinitely many higher brackets encoding the
n
-point amplitudes.
In the present setting, the analogue of the Lehmann-Symanzik-Zimmermann (LSZ) reduction formula is obtained by considering a basis of fields in
L[2]^{0}
that are
\ell^{\star}_{1}
-exact.

Throughout this paper we will mostly leave aside two important analytic issues to avoid clouding the main messages of this paper. Firstly, many of our formal manipulations can only be made precise when one uses wavepackets for the external particles, rather than delta-distributions. Secondly, we do not explicitly spell out regularisations of loop integrals, which are also needed to make sense of our algebraic manipulations. Both of these technical problems can be handled using standard quantum field theory techniques.

4.1
One-Point Functions

As a warm-up, let us start by computing the interacting one-point correlation functions using the homological perturbation lemma with the deformation retract (
3.41
), confirming that all tadpole diagrams vanish.

Using (
3.46
) and (
3.48
), the one-point photon correlator at one-loop in momentum space is calculated as

\begin{split}\mathsf{\tilde{G}}^{\hbar,{\rm int}}_{A_{\mu}}(p)^{\textrm{\tiny(1)}}&=\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,{\mathsf{\Delta}}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H}\,\big\{\mathcal{S}_{\rm int}^{{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}}\,,\,\mathsf{h}\,\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\mathtt{e}^{p}\big\}_{\star}\\[4.0pt]
&=\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,{\mathsf{\Delta}}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H}\,\int_{k_{1},k_{2},k_{3}}\,V_{3}^{\nu}(k_{1},k_{2},k_{3})\ \big\{\mathtt{v}_{\nu}\,\mathtt{e}^{k_{1}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{e}^{k_{2}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{k_{3}}\,,\,\mathsf{h}\,\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{p}\big\}_{\star}\\[4.0pt]
&=-\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,{\mathsf{\Delta}}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H}\,\int_{k_{1},k_{2},k_{3}}\,V_{3}^{\nu}(k_{1},k_{2},k_{3})\ \mathrm{e}^{\,\mathrm{i}\,(k_{2}+k_{3})\cdot\theta\,k_{1}}\,(2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(p+k_{1})\\
&\quad\,\hskip 227.62204pt\times\tilde{\mathsf{D}}(p)\,\tilde{\mathsf{\Pi}}_{\nu\mu}(p)\ \mathtt{e}^{k_{2}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{k_{3}}\\[4.0pt]
&=\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\int_{k_{1},k_{2},k_{3}}\,V_{3}^{\nu}(k_{1},k_{2},k_{3})\ (2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(k_{2}+k_{3})\,\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(k_{2})\,(2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(p+k_{1})\,\tilde{\mathsf{D}}(p)\,\tilde{\mathsf{\Pi}}_{\nu\mu}(p)\\[4.0pt]
&=2\,\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,g\,\int_{k}\,k^{\nu}\,\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(k)\,(2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(p)\,\tilde{\mathsf{D}}(p)\,\tilde{\mathsf{\Pi}}_{\nu\mu}(p)=0\ .\end{split}

(4.5)

In the last line we formally set
\int_{k}\,k^{\nu}\,\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(k)=0
, after reflection symmetric cutoff regularisation, because the integrand is an odd function of the loop
momentum. This vanishing contribution is represented graphically by the tadpole diagram

For the tadpoles of charged scalars at one-loop we find

\begin{split}\mathsf{\tilde{G}}^{\hbar,{\rm int}}_{\phi}(p)^{\textrm{\tiny(1)}}&=\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,{\mathsf{\Delta}}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H}\,\big\{\mathcal{S}_{\rm int}^{{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}}\,,\,\mathsf{h}\,\mathtt{e}^{p}\big\}_{\star}\\[4.0pt]
&=\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,{\mathsf{\Delta}}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H}\,\int_{k_{1},k_{2},k_{3}}\,V_{3}^{\nu}(k_{1},k_{2},k_{3})\ \big\{\mathtt{v}_{\nu}\,\mathtt{e}^{k_{1}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{e}^{k_{2}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{k_{3}}\,,\,\mathsf{h}\,\mathtt{e}^{p}\big\}_{\star}\\[4.0pt]
&=-\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,{\mathsf{\Delta}}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H}\,\int_{k_{1},k_{2},k_{3}}\,V_{3}^{\nu}(k_{1},k_{2},k_{3})\ (2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(p+k_{3})\,\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(p)\ \mathtt{v}_{\nu}\,\mathtt{e}^{k_{1}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{e}^{k_{2}}=0\ ,\end{split}

where the last line vanishes because there are no contractions between photons and scalars:

\displaystyle\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H}\,\big(\mathtt{v}_{\nu}\,\mathtt{e}^{k_{1}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{e}^{k_{2}}\big)=0\ .

(4.8)

Similarly,
\mathsf{\tilde{G}}^{\hbar,{\rm int}}_{\bar{\phi}}(p)^{\textrm{\tiny(1)}}=\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,{\mathsf{\Delta}}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H}\,\big\{\mathcal{S}_{\rm int}^{{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}}\,,\,\mathsf{h}\,\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{p}\big\}_{\star}=0

by the same argument.

4.2
Photon Vacuum Polarisation

Using the definition (
4.4
) of the
n
-point correlation function in momentum space, we now proceed to calculate the photon two-point function.

The tree-level photon two-point function is given by the leading order contribution in the homological perturbation lemma and coincides with the bare photon propagator:

\begin{split}\mathsf{\tilde{G}}^{\hbar}_{A_{\mu},A_{\nu}}(p_{1},p_{2})^{\textrm{\tiny(0)}}&=\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H}\,(\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{p_{1}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{v}_{\nu}\,\mathtt{e}^{p_{2}})\\[4.0pt]
&=-\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,(2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(p_{1}+p_{2})\,\mathsf{\tilde{D}}(p_{1})\,\mathsf{\tilde{\Pi}}_{\mu\nu}(p_{1})\\[4.0pt]
&=\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,(2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(p_{1}+p_{2})\,\frac{1}{p_{1}^{2}}\,\left(\eta_{\mu\nu}-\frac{p_{1\,\mu}\,p_{1\,\nu}}{p_{1}^{2}}\right)\ .\end{split}

(4.9)

At order
\hbar^{2}
, there are three terms that contribute to the two-point function. They are given by

\begin{split}\mathsf{\tilde{G}}^{\hbar,{\rm int}}_{A_{\mu},A_{\nu}}(p_{1},p_{2})^{\textrm{\tiny(1)}}&=(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H})^{2}\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int},\mathsf{H}\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int},\mathsf{H}\,(\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{p_{1}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{v}_{\nu}\,\mathtt{e}^{p_{2}})\right\}_{\star}\right\}_{\star}\\
&\quad\,+\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H}\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int},\mathsf{H}\,(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H})\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int},\mathsf{H}\,(\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{p_{1}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{v}_{\nu}\,\mathtt{e}^{p_{2}})\right\}_{\star}\right\}_{\star}\\
&\quad\,+(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H})^{2}\left\{\mathcal{S}_{\rm int}^{\textrm{\tiny(4)}},\mathsf{H}\,(\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{p_{1}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{v}_{\nu}\,\mathtt{e}^{p_{2}})\right\}_{\star}\\[4.0pt]
&=:\mathsf{\tilde{G}}_{\mu\nu}(p_{1},p_{2})_{\tt A}+\mathsf{\tilde{G}}_{\mu\nu}(p_{1},p_{2})_{\tt B}+\mathsf{\tilde{G}}_{\mu\nu}(p_{1},p_{2})_{\tt C}\ .\end{split}

(4.10)

Using the same techniques as for the calculation of tadpole diagrams in
section

4.1
, as well as in the analogue calculations for braided spinor QED detailed in
[
6
]
, we now calculate each of these three terms separately.

Compared to the one-point functions, the calculations for higher multiplicity correlators become increasingly more lengthy and cumbersome. They are simplified with the help of a diagrammatic calculus, similarly to those developed for (braided) scalar field theories in
[
5
,
7
]
, as well as in
[
38
]
for matrix models with gauge symmetries, which we employ below using the diagrammatic rules discussed in
section

3.2
. Throughout this paper, diagrams should be read from the bottom up, with input at the bottom and output at the top.
We explicitly add momentum labels in the initial instances and in final results, but otherwise mostly suppress them.

Evaluation of
{\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\tilde{G}}_{\mu\nu}(p_{1},p_{2})_{\tt A}}}
.

Denote the momentum space representation
\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{p_{1}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{v}_{\nu}\,\mathtt{e}^{p_{2}}
by two vertical photon lines.
Apply the three-vertex operator
\big\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int},-\big\}_{\star}\,\mathsf{H}:\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2]\longrightarrow\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2]
which is a strict derivation of total degree 0 by the discussion of
section

3.2
; however, it raises the symmetric degree by 1. This results in the non-zero terms

\begin{split}\bigg\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int}\,,\,\mathsf{H}\,\bigg(\,\vbox{\hbox{\hbox to23.12pt{\vbox to38.29pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 5.86928pt\lower-3.24522pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}

(4.13)

Note that any extra noncommutative phase factors can be removed by braiding the basis of antifields in the symmetric algebra. Contracting with
(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H})^{2}
discerns where the connected and disconnected diagrams originate.

Altogether one finds that all phase factors disappear and the first contribution to (
4.10
) results in

\begin{split}\mathsf{\tilde{G}}_{\mu\nu}(p_{1},p_{2})_{\tt A}&=-\hbar^{2}\,g^{2}\,\int_{k}\,(2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(p_{1}+p_{2})\,(p_{1}+2k)^{\lambda}\,(p_{1}+2k)^{\rho}\\
&\hskip 113.81102pt\times\tilde{\sf D}(p_{1})\,\tilde{\sf\Pi}_{\lambda\mu}(p_{1})\,\tilde{\sf D}(p_{2})\,\tilde{\sf\Pi}_{\rho\nu}(p_{2})\,\tilde{\sf G}(k)\,\tilde{\sf G}(k+p_{1})\\
&\quad\,-\frac{4\,\hbar^{2}\,g^{2}}{3}\,\int_{k,q}\,(2\pi)^{8}\,\delta(p_{1})\,\delta(p_{2})\,k^{\lambda}\,q^{\rho}\\
&\hskip 113.81102pt\times\tilde{\sf D}(p_{1})\,\tilde{\sf\Pi}_{\lambda\mu}(p_{1})\,\tilde{\sf D}(p_{2})\,\tilde{\sf\Pi}_{\rho\nu}(p_{2})\,\tilde{\sf G}(k)\,\tilde{\sf G}(q)\ .\end{split}

(4.14)

The first integral corresponds to the connected diagram

(4.17)

Further applying the operator
\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,{\mathsf{\Delta}}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H}\,\big\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int},-\big\}\,\mathsf{H}
gives another tadpole. In fact, as noted in
[
6
]
, this factorisation is also given in terms of one-point functions at one-loop from
section

4.1
.

Altogether the second contribution to (
4.10
) results in the same disconnected diagram (
4.16
), and hence has no contribution:

\mathsf{\tilde{G}}_{\mu\nu}(p_{1},p_{2})_{\tt B}=0
.

Evaluation of
{\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\tilde{G}}_{\mu\nu}(p_{1},p_{2})_{\tt C}}}
.

(4.18)

The contractions with
(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H})^{2}
are unambiguous and one can always jump across fields at the price of
R
-matrices, which in this instance end up trivialising due to momentum conservation.

Altogether the final result is represented graphically by the connected tadpole diagram

(4.19)

\mathsf{\tilde{G}}_{\mu\nu}(p_{1},p_{2})_{\tt C}=2\,\hbar^{2}\,g^{2}\,(2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(p_{1}+p_{2})\,\tilde{\sf D}(p_{1})\,\tilde{\sf\Pi}_{\lambda\mu}(p_{1})\,\tilde{\sf D}(p_{2})\,\tilde{\sf\Pi}^{\lambda}_{\ \nu}(p_{2})\,\int_{k}\,\tilde{\sf G}(k)\ .

(4.20)

Photon Self-Energy.

The photon two-point function at one-loop receives contributions from only bubble diagrams, and adding the contributions gives

\begin{split}\mathsf{\tilde{G}}^{\hbar,{\rm int}}_{A_{\mu},A_{\nu}}(p_{1},p_{2})^{\textrm{\tiny(1)}}&=(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,g)^{2}\,(2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(p_{1}+p_{2})\,\tilde{\mathsf{\Pi}}_{\mu\lambda}(p_{1})\,\tilde{\mathsf{D}}(p_{1})\,\tilde{\mathsf{\Pi}}_{\nu\rho}(p_{2})\,\tilde{\mathsf{D}}(p_{2})\\
&\quad\,\times\int_{k}\,\left((2k+p_{1})^{\lambda}\,(2k+p_{1})^{\rho}\,\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(k+p_{1})\,\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(k)-2\,\eta^{\lambda\rho}\,\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(k)\right)\ .\end{split}

(4.21)

Equivalently, one can dress the photon propagator of (
4.9
) in terms of the one-loop photon vacuum polarisation tensor
{\Pi}_{\star}(p)^{\textrm{\tiny(1)}}
by setting

\mathsf{\tilde{G}}^{\hbar}_{A_{\mu},A_{\nu}}(p_{1},p_{2})^{\textrm{\tiny(0)}}+\mathsf{\tilde{G}}^{\hbar,{\rm int}}_{A_{\mu},A_{\nu}}(p_{1},p_{2})^{\textrm{\tiny(1)}}=\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,(2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(p_{1}+p_{2})\,\left(\frac{1}{p_{1}^{2}\,\mathsf{\tilde{\Pi}}^{-1}(p_{1})-{\Pi}_{\star}(p_{1})^{\textrm{\tiny(1)}}}\right)_{\mu\nu}\ ,

(4.22)

where the transverse projector
\mathsf{\tilde{\Pi}}(k)
is given by (
2.20
). This coincides with the commutative result

\lxSVG@closescope
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}\\[4.0pt]
&=g^{2}\,\int_{k}\,\frac{(2k+p)^{\mu}\,(2k+p)^{\nu}}{\big((k+p)^{2}-m^{2}\big)\,\big(k^{2}-m^{2}\big)}-2\,g^{2}\,\int_{k}\,\frac{\eta^{\mu\nu}}{(k+p)^{2}-m^{2}}\ .\end{split}

(4.23)

Since the loop diagrams here reproduce the commutative results, this implies that there is no UV/IR mixing in the photon vacuum polarisation at the one-loop level. This raises hopes that our braided field theory is perturbatively renormalisable and so has a good quantum theory. In particular, like the free photon propagator, after dimensional regularisation the one-loop polarisation tensor is transverse:

\displaystyle p_{\mu}\,\Pi_{\star}^{\mu\nu}(p)^{\textrm{\tiny(1)}}=0\ .

(4.24)

An easy but formal way to argue this is by using the identity

\displaystyle p\cdot(2k+p)=\big((k+p)^{2}-m^{2}\big)-\big(k^{2}-m^{2}\big)

(4.25)

and shifting integration variable
k\longmapsto k-p
in two of the three resulting integrals from (
4.23
).

4.3
Scalar Vacuum Polarisation

The tree-level two-point function for the charged scalar field follows from (
4.4
) and is given by

\begin{split}\mathsf{\tilde{G}}^{\hbar}_{\phi,\bar{\phi}}(p_{1},p_{2})^{\textrm{\tiny(0)}}&=\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H}\,(\mathtt{e}^{p_{1}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{p_{2}})\\[4.0pt]
&=-\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,(2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(p_{1}+p_{2})\,\mathsf{\tilde{G}}(p_{1})\\[4.0pt]
&=-\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,(2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(p_{1}+p_{2})\ \frac{1}{p_{1}^{2}-m^{2}}\ .\end{split}

(4.26)

Similarly to the photon two-point function at one-loop, the homological perturbation lemma gives three terms contributing the scalar two-point function at one-loop. These are given by

\begin{split}\mathsf{\tilde{G}}^{\hbar,{\rm int}}_{\phi,\bar{\phi}}(p_{1},p_{2})^{\textrm{\tiny(1)}}&=(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,{\mathsf{\Delta}}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H})^{2}\left\{\mathcal{S}_{\rm int}^{{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}},\mathsf{H}\left\{\mathcal{S}_{\rm int}^{{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}},\mathsf{H}\,(\mathtt{e}^{p_{1}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{p_{2}})\right\}_{\star}\right\}_{\star}\\
&\quad\,+\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,{\mathsf{\Delta}}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H}\left\{\mathcal{S}_{\rm int}^{{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}},\mathsf{H}\,(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,{\mathsf{\Delta}}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H})\left\{\mathcal{S}_{\rm int}^{{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}},\mathsf{H}\,(\mathtt{e}^{p_{1}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{p_{2}})\right\}_{\star}\right\}_{\star}\\
&\quad\,+(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,{\mathsf{\Delta}}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H})^{2}\left\{\mathcal{S}_{\rm int}^{{\textrm{\tiny(4)}}},\mathsf{H}\,(\mathtt{e}^{p_{1}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{p_{2}})\right\}_{\star}\\[4.0pt]
&=:\mathsf{\tilde{G}}(p_{1},p_{2})_{\tt A}+\mathsf{\tilde{G}}(p_{1},p_{2})_{\tt B}+\mathsf{\tilde{G}}(p_{1},p_{2})_{\tt C}\ .\end{split}

(4.27)

{\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\tilde{G}}(p_{1},p_{2})_{\tt A}}}

(4.31)

They respectively sum to

\begin{split}\mathsf{\tilde{G}}(p_{1},p_{2})_{\tt A}&=-\hbar^{2}\,g^{2}\,(2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(p_{1}+p_{2})\,\mathsf{\tilde{G}}(p_{1})\,\mathsf{\tilde{G}}(p_{2})\\
&\hskip 142.26378pt\times\int_{k}\,(k+2p_{1})^{\mu}\,(k+2p_{1})^{\nu}\,\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(k+p_{1})\,\tilde{\mathsf{D}}(k)\,\tilde{\mathsf{\Pi}}_{\mu\nu}(k)\\
&\quad\,-\frac{4\,\hbar^{2}\,g^{2}}{3}\,\int_{k,q}\,(2\pi)^{8}\,\delta(p_{1}+p_{2})\,\delta(k)\,\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(p_{1})\,\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(p_{2})\,\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(q)\,\tilde{\mathsf{D}}(k)\,\tilde{\mathsf{\Pi}}_{\mu\nu}(k)\,p_{1}^{\mu}\,q^{\nu}\ .\end{split}

(4.32)

The second integral is a tadpole contribution which vanishes by
section

4.1
, leaving only the contribution from the first integral. The noncommutative phase coming from the vertex in (
3.9
) vanishes due to momentum conservation.

Evaluation of
{\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\tilde{G}}(p_{1},p_{2})_{\tt B}}}
.

The second contribution to (
4.27
) is the same scalar tadpole diagram (
4.31
). This is most easily seen by following the symmetric degree inside the calculation. The application of
\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,{\mathsf{\Delta}}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H}
to (
4.28
) has symmetric degree
1
, involving the field
\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{k_{1}}
, so further applying
\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,{\mathsf{\Delta}}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H}\,\big\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int}\ ,-\big\}\,\mathsf{H}
closes a tadpole, thereby giving a vanishing contribution to the scalar two-point function at one-loop:

\mathsf{\tilde{G}}(p_{1},p_{2})_{\tt B}=0
.

) disappears as before because of momentum conservation.

\lxSVG@closescope }
\lxSVG@closescope } \normalsize
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\end{split}

(4.34)

The explicit result is

\mathsf{\tilde{G}}(p_{1},p_{2})_{\tt C}=-3\,\hbar^{2}\,g^{2}\,(2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(p_{1}+p_{2})\,\mathsf{\tilde{G}}(p_{1})\,\mathsf{\tilde{G}}(p_{2})\,\int_{k}\,\tilde{\mathsf{D}}(k)\ .

(4.35)

Scalar Self-Energy.

Altogether we find that the charged scalar field two-point function at one-loop is given by

\displaystyle\begin{split}\tilde{\mathsf{G}}^{\hbar,{\rm int}}_{\phi,\bar{\phi}}(p_{1},p_{2})^{\textrm{\tiny(1)}}&=(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,g)^{2}\,(2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(p_{1}+p_{2})\,\mathsf{\tilde{G}}(p_{1})\,\mathsf{\tilde{G}}(p_{2})\\
&\quad\,\times\int_{k}\,\left((k+2p_{1})^{\mu}\,(k+2p_{1})^{\nu}\,\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(k+p_{1})\,\tilde{\mathsf{D}}(k)\,\tilde{\mathsf{\Pi}}_{\mu\nu}(k)-3\,\mathsf{\tilde{D}}(k)\right)\ .\end{split}

(4.36)

The dressed scalar propagator at one-loop is defined by

\tilde{\mathsf{G}}^{\hbar}_{\phi,\bar{\phi}}(p_{1},p_{2})^{\textrm{\tiny(0)}}+\tilde{\mathsf{G}}^{\hbar,{\rm int}}_{\phi,\bar{\phi}}(p_{1},p_{2})^{\textrm{\tiny(1)}}=-\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,(2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(p_{1}+p_{2})\ \frac{1}{p_{1}^{2}-m^{2}-{\Sigma}_{\star}(p_{1})^{\textrm{\tiny(1)}}}\ ,

(4.37)

where the self-energy
\Sigma_{\star}(p)^{\textrm{\tiny(1)}}
is obtained by removing external scalar propagators
\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(p)
and is the sum of amputated diagrams

&=-g^{2}\,\int_{k}\,\frac{(k+2p)^{\mu}\,(k+2p)^{\nu}}{k^{2}\,\big((k+p)^{2}-m^{2}\big)}\,\left(\eta_{\mu\nu}-\frac{k_{\mu}\,k_{\nu}}{k^{2}}\right)-3\,g^{2}\,\int_{k}\,\frac{1}{k^{2}}\ .\end{split}

(4.38)

In summary, we recover the commutative result for the charged scalar field self-energy and no UV/IR mixing.

4.4
Three-Vertex Function

The three-vertex function at tree-level is

\begin{split}\mathsf{\tilde{G}}^{\hbar,{\rm int}}_{\phi,\bar{\phi},A_{\mu}}(p_{1},p_{2},p_{3})^{\textrm{\tiny(0)}}&=(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H})^{2}\,\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\mathrm{int}}\,,\,\mathsf{H}\,(\mathtt{e}^{p_{1}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{p_{2}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{p_{3}})\right\}_{\star}\\[4.0pt]
&=-(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar)^{2}\,V^{\lambda}_{3}(p_{3},-p_{2},-p_{1})\,\mathsf{\tilde{G}}(p_{1})\,\mathsf{\tilde{G}}(p_{2})\,\mathsf{\tilde{D}}(p_{3})\,\mathsf{\tilde{\Pi}}_{\lambda\mu}(p_{3})\\
&\qquad\,+\tfrac{1}{3}\,\mathsf{\tilde{G}}^{\hbar,{\rm int}}_{A_{\mu}}(p_{3})^{\textrm{\tiny(1)}}\,\mathsf{\tilde{G}}^{\hbar}_{\phi,\bar{\phi}}(p_{1},p_{2})^{\textrm{\tiny(0)}}\ .\end{split}

(4.39)

The last line is proportional to the photon one-point function at one-loop, which we found to vanish in (
4.5
). Hence

\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathsf{\tilde{G}}^{\hbar,{\rm int}}_{\phi,\bar{\phi},A_{\mu}}(p_{1},p_{2},p_{3})^{\textrm{\tiny(0)}}&=-\hbar^{2}\,g\,(2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(p_{3}-p_{1}-p_{2})\\
&\qquad\,\times\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2}\,\sum\limits_{i<j}\,p_{i}\cdot\theta\,p_{j}}\,\frac{(p_{1}-p_{2})^{\lambda}}{\big(p_{1}^{2}-m^{2}\big)\,\big(p_{2}^{2}-m^{2}\big)}\,\frac{1}{p_{3}^{2}}\,\left(\eta_{\lambda\mu}-\frac{p_{3\,\lambda}\,p_{3\,\mu}}{p_{3}^{2}}\right)\ ,\end{split}

(4.40)

which differs from the commutative result by the phase factor depending on the external momenta.

We shall now detail the calculation of the three-point vertex at one-loop order.
For this, one needs to calculate the combinations of interactions and contractions, omitting obvious tadpole terms which vanish.
We recall the degrees of relevant operators, which are useful in identifying contributions that are obviously zero:

Operator

Symmetric Degree

\big\{\mathcal{S}^{{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}}_{\mathrm{int}},-\big\}_{\star}\,\mathsf{H}

+1

\big\{\mathcal{S}^{{\textrm{\tiny(4)}}}_{\mathrm{int}},-\big\}_{\star}\,\mathsf{H}

+2

\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H}

-2

(4.41)

The term

\begin{split}\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H}\,\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int}\,,\,\mathsf{H}\,(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H})^{2}\,\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int}\,,\,\mathsf{H}\,\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int}\ ,\ \mathsf{H}\,(\mathtt{e}^{p_{1}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{p_{2}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{p_{3}})\right\}_{\star}\right\}_{\star}\right\}_{\star}=0\end{split}

(4.42)

vanishes by symmetric power counting:
After the application of
(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H})^{2}
we end up with a monomial in the symmetric algebra, which then leads to a vanishing tadpole diagram by
section

4.1
.
Several other terms vanish similarly.
Note that any operator landing in symmetric degree 0, for example

(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H})^{2}\,\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int}\ ,\ \mathsf{H}\,(\mathtt{e}^{p_{1}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{p_{2}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{v}_{\nu}\,\mathtt{e}^{p_{3}})\right\}_{\star}\ \in\ \big(\mathrm{Sym}_{\star}L[2]\big)^{0}\ ,

(4.43)

yields a vanishing contribution.
The upshot is that terms where the contraction operator
\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H}
acts early enough vanish, and we omit them from now on.

The manifestly non-zero
\mathsf{P}_{0}
-projections that contribute to the one-loop three-point function

\displaystyle\mathsf{\tilde{G}}^{\hbar,{\rm int}}_{\phi,\bar{\phi},A_{\mu}}(p_{1},p_{2},p_{3})^{\textrm{\tiny(1)}}={\text{\small{\tt(I)}}}+{\text{\small{\tt(II)}}}+{\text{\small{\tt(III)}}}+{\text{\small{\tt(IV)}}}+{\text{\small{\tt(V)}}}+{\text{\small{\tt(VI)}}}+{\text{\small{\tt(VII)}}}

(4.44)

are given by

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt{\text{\small{\tt(I)}}}=(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H})^{2}\,\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int}\,,\,\mathsf{H}\,\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int}\,,\,\mathsf{H}\,(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H})\,\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int}\ ,\ \mathsf{H}\,(\mathtt{e}^{p_{1}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{p_{2}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{p_{3}})\right\}_{\star}\right\}_{\star}\right\}_{\star}\ ,

(4.45a)

\displaystyle\hskip-5.69046pt{\text{\small{\tt(II)}}}=(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H})^{2}\,\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int}\,,\,\mathsf{H}\,(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H})\,\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int}\,,\,\mathsf{H}\,\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int}\ ,\ \mathsf{H}\,(\mathtt{e}^{p_{1}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{p_{2}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{p_{3}})\right\}_{\star}\right\}_{\star}\right\}_{\star}\ ,

(4.45b)

\displaystyle\hskip-11.38092pt{\text{\small{\tt(III)}}}=(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H})^{3}\,\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int}\,,\,\mathsf{H}\,\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int}\,,\,\mathsf{H}\,\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int}\ ,\ \mathsf{H}\,(\mathtt{e}^{p_{1}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{p_{2}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{p_{3}})\right\}_{\star}\right\}_{\star}\right\}_{\star}\ ,

(4.45c)

\displaystyle\hskip-5.69046pt{\text{\small{\tt(IV)}}}=(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H})^{2}\,\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(4)}}_{\rm int}\,,\,\mathsf{H}\,(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H})\,\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int}\ ,\ \mathsf{H}\,(\mathtt{e}^{p_{1}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{p_{2}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{p_{3}})\right\}_{\star}\right\}_{\star}\ ,

(4.45d)

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt{\text{\small{\tt(V)}}}=(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H})^{3}\,\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int}\,,\,\mathsf{H}\,\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(4)}}_{\rm int}\ ,\ \mathsf{H}\,(\mathtt{e}^{p_{1}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{p_{2}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{p_{3}})\right\}_{\star}\right\}_{\star}\ ,

(4.45e)

\displaystyle\hskip-5.69046pt{\text{\small{\tt(VI)}}}=(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H})^{3}\,\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(4)}}_{\rm int}\,,\,\mathsf{H}\,\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int}\ ,\ \mathsf{H}\,(\mathtt{e}^{p_{1}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{p_{2}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{p_{3}})\right\}_{\star}\right\}_{\star}\ ,

(4.45f)

\displaystyle\hskip-11.38092pt{\text{\small{\tt(VII)}}}=(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H})^{2}\,\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(3)}}_{\rm int}\,,\,\mathsf{H}\,(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar\,\mathsf{\Delta}_{\textrm{\tiny BV}}\,\mathsf{H})\,\left\{\mathcal{S}^{\textrm{\tiny(4)}}_{\rm int}\ ,\ \mathsf{H}\,(\mathtt{e}^{p_{1}}\odot_{\star}\bar{\mathtt{e}}^{p_{2}}\odot_{\star}\mathtt{v}_{\mu}\,\mathtt{e}^{p_{3}})\right\}_{\star}\right\}_{\star}\ .

(4.45g)

In the remainder of this section we summarise the results of these computations.

) and (

) will come from a later term.
The explicit analytic expressions for these and other diagrams are summarised at the end of this section.

Calculation of
(II)
.

In the rest of this section we will not draw all diagrams; one can find the relevant contributions following the procedure outlined above.
The second term
(II)
from (
4.45b
) contributes to the one-particle irreducible (1PI) part of the correlation function.

(4.50)

With the vertex function (
3.9
), we notice that the phase factor appearing in (
4.50
) combines with the phase factors appearing in the vertex function to factor out of the loop integral.
This is nothing but the corresponding commutative diagram dressed by an external phase factor.

Calculation of
(III)
.

The 1PI part of the third term
(III)
from (
4.45c
) is of the same form as the triangle diagram contribution to (
4.50
).
Altogether, its contributions sum up to

\begin{split}{\text{\small{\tt(III)}}}\ =\ \frac{3}{2}\,\times\,{\text{\small{\tt(II)}}}\end{split}

(4.51)

which is just the commutative result times the external phase factor.

(4.53)

together with

\displaystyle{\text{\small{\tt(VI)}}}\ =\ \frac{5}{6}\,\times\,{\text{\small{\tt(V)}}}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad{\text{\small{\tt(VII)}}}\ =\ \frac{2}{3}\,\times\,{\text{\small{\tt(V)}}}\ .

(4.54)

This is the commutative result up to the external noncommutative phase factor.

One-Loop Corrections to the Three-Vertex.

The three-vertex correction corresponds to the contributions from 1PI diagrams.
Combining the above results, we obtain the 1PI three-point correlation function

}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{16.32605pt}{-10.2859pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform=matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 22.59 -14.23)} \pgfsys@hbox{58}\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}}\normalsize\quad\right)\end{split}

(4.55)

Using the expressions for the diagrams below, this reads explicitly

\begin{split}&\mathsf{\tilde{G}}^{\hbar,{\rm int}}_{\phi,\phi^{\dagger},A_{\mu}}(p_{1},p_{2},p_{3})_{\text{\tiny 1PI}}^{\textrm{\tiny(1)}}\\[4.0pt]
&\hskip 28.45274pt=g^{3}\,(\mathrm{i}\,\hbar)^{3}\,\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2}\,\sum\limits_{i<j}\,p_{i}\cdot\theta\,p_{j}}\,\mathsf{\tilde{G}}(p_{1})\,\mathsf{\tilde{G}}(p_{2})\,\mathsf{\tilde{D}}(p_{3})\,\mathsf{\tilde{\Pi}}_{\rho\mu}(p_{3})\,(2\pi)^{4}\,\delta(p_{1}+p_{2}-p_{3})\\
&\hskip 56.9055pt\,\times\bigg(\int_{k}\,(k-2p_{1})^{\lambda}\,(k+2p_{2})^{\alpha}\,(-2k+p_{1}-p_{2})^{\rho}\,\\
&\hskip 213.39566pt\times\mathsf{\tilde{G}}(k-p_{1})\,\mathsf{\tilde{G}}(k+p_{2})\,\mathsf{\tilde{D}}(k)\,\mathsf{\tilde{\Pi}}_{\lambda\alpha}(k)\\
&\hskip 85.35826pt-2\,\int_{k}\,\eta^{\lambda\rho}\,\left((k+2p_{2})^{\alpha}\,\mathsf{\tilde{G}}(k+p_{2})\,\mathsf{\tilde{D}}(k)\,\mathsf{\tilde{\Pi}}_{\alpha\lambda}(k)\right.\\
&\hskip 213.39566pt\left.-\,(k+2p_{1})^{\alpha}\,\mathsf{\tilde{G}}(k+p_{1})\,\mathsf{\tilde{D}}(k)\,\mathsf{\tilde{\Pi}}_{\lambda\alpha}(k)\right)\bigg)\ .\end{split}

(4.56)
